ethylene.label: Ethylene gas
ethylene.blurb: A ripening gas given off by apples, bananas, avocados, tomatoes and other fruit. Sensitive produce yellows, spots or turns bitter around it.

ripening.label: Overripening
ripening.blurb: The fruit keeps ripening after you buy it, driven by its own ethylene, until it goes past its best.

moisture_loss.label: Drying out
moisture_loss.blurb: Produce keeps losing water after harvest. Dry fridge air speeds it up, and nothing replaces what is lost.

excess_moisture.label: Trapped moisture
excess_moisture.blurb: Wet surfaces and sealed containers give bacteria and mold the damp conditions they need.

mold.label: Mold
mold.blurb: Fungi such as gray mold. Some grow slowly even at refrigerator temperatures.

bacterial_rot.label: Bacterial rot
bacterial_rot.blurb: Soft-rot bacteria break tissue down into wet, slimy patches, usually starting where it was bruised, cut or frozen.

chilling.label: Too cold
chilling.blurb: Tropical and warm-season produce is damaged by temperatures that are normal for a fridge, even without freezing.

bruising.label: Bruising
bruising.blurb: Bumps and crushing break cells open. The damaged spot browns and is where rot gets in.

age.label: Age
age.blurb: Produce is still alive after harvest. It slowly uses up its stored sugar and water, even when stored well.

light.label: Light
light.blurb: Light turns potatoes green and builds up solanine, a bitter natural toxin. Dark storage prevents it.

eat.label: Still good
eat.blurb: Safe and fine to eat, maybe after a quick fix.

cook.label: Cook it soon
cook.blurb: Safe, but past its best raw. Cook it or blend it in the next day or two.

trim.label: Trim and use
trim.blurb: Cut away the damaged part and use the rest soon.

toss.label: Toss it
toss.blurb: Not worth the risk. Compost it if you can.

items.name: Lettuce
items.intro: Romaine and leaf lettuce usually fail in one of three ways: brown specks from ethylene, limp leaves from drying out, or slime from bacteria. Only the last one means it's done.

failures.title: Brown or rusty specks on the ribs
failures.symptom: Small tan-to-brown spots, mostly along the pale midribs of romaine and leaf lettuce.
failures.why: This is russet spotting. Romaine reacts to as little as 1 part per million of ethylene, the gas apples, pears, bananas and tomatoes give off. A shared crisper drawer can easily reach that.
prevent: Give lettuce its own drawer, away from apples, pears, bananas and tomatoes
Store it unwashed in a bag lined with paper towels
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat. The spots can taste a little bitter, so trim the worst ribs if they bother you.
rescue: Shred it into tacos, wraps or fried rice, where the spots won't show
Halve romaine hearts and char them in a hot pan or on the grill

failures.title: Limp, floppy leaves
failures.symptom: Leaves bend instead of snapping, and the edges look thin or papery.
failures.why: Lettuce has a lot of leaf surface and loses water quickly. Dry fridge air, or a bag left open, pulls moisture out of it.
prevent: Keep it in the crisper drawer on the humid setting
Wrap it loosely in a damp (not wet) paper towel inside a bag
failures.verdictNote: Still good. Limp lettuce is only thirsty, and it usually firms back up.
rescue: Soak the leaves in ice water for 15 to 30 minutes, then spin them dry
Wilt limp outer leaves into soup or a stir-fry

failures.title: Dark, wet, slimy leaves
failures.symptom: Translucent or dark green patches that feel slick, often with a sour smell.
failures.why: Soft-rot bacteria take hold in leaves that are damaged, wet or frozen. Lettuce pushed against the back wall of the fridge can freeze, and those leaves turn slimy fast once they thaw. Rot spreads faster when it's warm and humid.
prevent: Dry leaves well before storing, and keep a paper towel in the bag to catch condensation
Keep lettuce away from the back wall of the fridge, where it can freeze
Pull off damaged outer leaves before they spread decay
failures.verdictNote: Toss the slimy leaves and the ones touching them. If the bag smells off or most of it is slimy, toss the whole thing.

items.name: Spinach
items.intro: Spinach goes yellow from ethylene, wilts as it dries out, and turns slimy when bacteria get into crushed or wet leaves. Yellow and wilted spinach is still good for cooking.

failures.title: Leaves turning yellow
failures.symptom: Leaves fade from dark green to pale or yellow, starting at the edges or with the oldest leaves.
failures.why: Spinach is highly sensitive to ethylene, and even low levels make the leaves yellow faster. Fruit in the same drawer is the usual source.
prevent: Keep spinach away from apples, bananas, tomatoes and peaches
Store it in a container lined with paper towels
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat. Yellow leaves taste flatter, so they're better cooked than in a salad.
rescue: Wilt it into eggs, pasta or soup
Blend it into a smoothie or pesto

failures.title: Wet, dark, slimy leaves
failures.symptom: Leaves clump together, look dark and wet, and may smell sour.
failures.why: Bacterial soft rot usually starts on crushed stems and damaged leaves. A packed clamshell bruises leaves, and condensation gives bacteria the moisture they need. Spinach also freezes just below 32°F, and frozen leaves rot quickly after they thaw.
prevent: Don't pack it down. Give leaves room in the container
Line the container with a paper towel and replace it if it gets wet
Keep spinach away from the back wall of the fridge
failures.verdictNote: Pick out and toss slimy leaves, plus any stuck to them. If the container smells off, toss it all.

failures.title: Wilted, droopy leaves
failures.symptom: Leaves have gone soft and floppy but are still green and dry.
failures.why: Spinach leaves are thin and lose water fast. An open bag in dry fridge air speeds that up.
prevent: Keep the container closed, with a paper towel inside
Store it in the high-humidity crisper drawer
failures.verdictNote: Still good to cook, since spinach wilts in the pan anyway.
rescue: Sauté it with garlic and olive oil
Freeze it in a bag to drop into smoothies or soups

items.name: Kale
items.intro: Kale keeps longer than most greens when it's cold, but it yellows around ethylene and loses water quickly. Neither one makes it unsafe.

failures.title: Leaves turning yellow
failures.symptom: Leaves lose their deep green color and turn yellow, often from the tips inward.
failures.why: Kale produces very little ethylene but is sensitive to it, and exposure turns the leaves yellow. Warm storage makes it worse.
prevent: Keep kale away from apples and bananas
Store it cold, in a bag with a little air
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat. Yellow leaves are more bitter, so cook them instead of eating them raw.
rescue: Simmer it into soups and stews
Blanch and freeze it for later

failures.title: Limp or leathery leaves
failures.symptom: Leaves droop and feel soft or leathery instead of crisp.
failures.why: Kale loses water fast. In one study, kale lost more than half its fresh weight in six days at room temperature, faster than broccoli or cabbage.
prevent: Wrap it in a damp paper towel inside a bag
Get it into the fridge soon after you buy it
failures.verdictNote: Still good. Soak it in cold water for 15 minutes to firm it back up for salads, or just cook it.
rescue: Bake it into kale chips
Blend it into pesto or a smoothie

items.name: Broccoli
items.intro: Broccoli is one of the most ethylene-sensitive vegetables you can buy. Yellow florets are the classic sign. It can also dry out or rot, especially at the cut stem.

failures.title: Florets turning yellow
failures.symptom: The tiny buds on the florets turn from dark green to yellow, starting at the edges of the head.
failures.why: Ethylene speeds up floret yellowing. UC Davis reports that 2 parts per million of ethylene at 50°F cuts broccoli's shelf life in half. Apples, bananas, peaches and tomatoes nearby are the usual source.
prevent: Keep broccoli away from apples, bananas, peaches and tomatoes
Store it cold, unwashed, in a loose bag in the crisper
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat but more bitter. Roasting or soup hides it best.
rescue: Roast it hot with lemon and parmesan
Blend it into broccoli soup

failures.title: Rubbery, bendy stems
failures.symptom: The stalk bends instead of snapping, and the florets feel soft.
failures.why: Broccoli keeps losing water after harvest. A tightly sealed bag isn't the answer, because it traps moisture and invites rot. A damp wrap on the stem works better.
prevent: Wrap the stem end in a damp paper towel
Use a loose bag, not a sealed one
failures.verdictNote: Still good. Trim the stem end and stand it in cold water for an hour to firm it up.
rescue: Peel the stalk and slice it into stir-fry coins

failures.title: Dark, soft or fuzzy spots
failures.symptom: Brown or black soft spots, a slimy patch, or gray or black fuzz on the florets or cut stem.
failures.why: Bacterial soft rot, gray mold and black mold are the main causes of broccoli decay. They usually start where the head was damaged or got wet.
prevent: Don't wash it until you're ready to cook
Use it within a few days of buying it
failures.verdictNote: A small spot on the thick stalk can be cut out with an inch to spare around it. If the florets are moldy or slimy, toss the head.

items.name: Cucumber
items.intro: Cucumbers are tricky: a regular fridge is colder than they like, and they're sensitive to ethylene too. Most problems come from those two things.

failures.title: Watery spots and pits in the skin
failures.symptom: Sunken pits or dark, water-soaked patches on the skin, sometimes followed by soft, rotting spots.
failures.why: This is chilling injury. Cucumbers are damaged below 50°F if they stay there more than one to three days, and most fridges run around 37°F to 40°F. The damage adds up over time and makes rot more likely.
prevent: Keep them in the warmest part of the fridge, in the door or at the front
Wrap each one in a paper towel, then loosely in a bag
Buy only what you'll use within a few days
failures.verdictNote: If the cucumber is still firm, cut off the pitted spots and use it soon. If it's soft, slimy or moldy, toss it.
rescue: Make quick refrigerator pickles
Grate it into tzatziki

failures.title: Skin turning yellow
failures.symptom: Green skin fades to yellow, and the cucumber may get seedy or bitter.
failures.why: Cucumbers are highly sensitive to ethylene. 1 to 5 parts per million speeds up yellowing and decay, which is why UC Davis says not to store them with bananas, melons or tomatoes.
prevent: Keep them away from bananas, melons, tomatoes and apples
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat. Peel it if the skin tastes bitter.
rescue: Peel and blend it into gazpacho or a smoothie
Make quick pickles

failures.title: Soft, slimy or moldy
failures.symptom: The cucumber goes soft and mushy, leaks, feels slimy, or shows mold.
failures.why: Bacteria and fungi cause most cucumber losses, especially after chilling injury has weakened the skin.
prevent: Avoid the coldest parts of the fridge
Keep them dry
failures.verdictNote: Toss it. USDA lists cucumbers as soft produce, where mold can spread below the surface, so cutting it away isn't enough.

items.name: Carrot
items.intro: Carrots last for weeks, so when they fail, it's usually because they dried out or picked up a bitter taste from ethylene. Both are fixable.

failures.title: Bitter taste
failures.symptom: The carrots look fine but taste bitter or soapy.
failures.why: Ethylene makes carrots produce a bitter compound. As little as 0.5 parts per million can cause noticeable bitterness within two weeks. An apple in the same drawer is enough.
prevent: Keep carrots away from apples, pears and other fruit
Store them in a bag in the crisper drawer
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat. Cooking them with something sweet balances the bitterness.
rescue: Roast or glaze them with honey or maple
Blend them into carrot-ginger soup

failures.title: Bendy, rubbery carrots
failures.symptom: Carrots bend without snapping and may look shriveled.
failures.why: Carrots go rubbery when they lose water. Green tops left on keep pulling moisture out of the root.
prevent: Cut off green tops before storing
Keep them in a closed bag, or in a container of water in the fridge
failures.verdictNote: Still good. Soak them in cold water for an hour to firm them back up.
rescue: Grate them into slaw, muffins or fritters
Simmer them in soup or stock

failures.title: White film on baby carrots
failures.symptom: Peeled baby carrots look chalky or whitish.
failures.why: This is white blush: the cut, peeled surface drying out. It's cosmetic.
prevent: Keep the bag sealed between uses
failures.verdictNote: Still good. Rinse them or soak them in water for a few minutes and the color comes back.

failures.title: Moldy or slimy spots
failures.symptom: Fuzzy patches, or soft, wet, slimy areas, often at the tip or crown.
failures.why: Gray mold, watery rot and bacterial soft rot all attack carrots, and standing water in the bag helps them along.
prevent: Keep the bag free of standing water
Check stored carrots every week or so
failures.verdictNote: Carrots are firm, so USDA says a small mold spot can be cut off with at least an inch around and below it. If a carrot is slimy or soft all the way through, toss it.

items.name: Celery
items.intro: Celery mostly fails by drying out. It's less sensitive to ethylene than most greens, and when it does rot, it starts at the cut ends.

failures.title: Limp, bendy stalks
failures.symptom: Stalks bend instead of snapping.
failures.why: Celery keeps best at very high humidity, close to 100%. Fridge air is much drier, so uncovered celery wilts.
prevent: Wrap it in aluminum foil, or keep cut stalks in a jar of water
Store it whole in the crisper drawer
failures.verdictNote: Still good. Trim the base and stand the stalks in cold water for an hour.
rescue: Add it to soup, stock or stir-fry

failures.title: Stalks losing their green color
failures.symptom: Stalks fade from green to pale or yellowish.
failures.why: Celery isn't very sensitive to ethylene when it's cold. At higher levels and warmer temperatures, though, it loses its green color.
prevent: Keep it away from apples and pears
Keep it cold
failures.verdictNote: Still good. The color is cosmetic.

failures.title: Hollow, spongy or white inside
failures.symptom: The inside of the stalk is white, dry and spongy instead of solid.
failures.why: This is pith breakdown, linked to age, cold stress and water stress, sometimes starting before harvest.
prevent: Use older bunches first
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat. The texture is poor raw but fine in cooking.
rescue: Chop it into soup, stock or a soffritto

failures.title: Slimy ends or moldy stalks
failures.symptom: Cut ends turn brown and slimy, or stalks show fuzzy gray or white mold.
failures.why: Cut stalks are especially prone to bacterial rot. Gray mold and watery rot can develop over a few weeks even in a cold fridge.
prevent: Store celery whole, and cut it when you need it
Change the water every couple of days if you keep cut stalks in water
failures.verdictNote: Toss slimy or moldy stalks. Other stalks from the bunch are fine if they're firm and smell normal.

items.name: Herbs (Fresh)
items.intro: Herbs aren't all the same. Basil hates the cold, parsley and mint yellow around ethylene, and cilantro rots fast if it's wet.

failures.title: Basil leaves turning black
failures.symptom: Basil leaves get dark brown or black patches, often within a day or two of going in the fridge.
failures.why: Basil and shiso are the only common herbs that are damaged by cold, and UC Davis says to keep them above 50°F. Research has found basil leaves blacken in as little as one day at 32°F, or three days at 41°F.
prevent: Keep basil on the counter, stems in a glass of water, out of direct sun
failures.verdictNote: Cold damage isn't a safety problem, but black leaves won't recover. Pick them off and use the rest today.
rescue: Blend the good leaves into pesto and freeze it in an ice-cube tray

failures.title: Parsley, mint or cilantro turning yellow
failures.symptom: Leaves turn yellow, stems curl, and leaves drop.
failures.why: Ethylene causes yellowing, curling and leaf drop in herbs. UC Davis lists marjoram, mint, parsley and oregano as very sensitive. Sage, thyme, basil and rosemary barely react.
prevent: Keep herb jars on a different shelf from apples, bananas and tomatoes
Trim stems and stand tender herbs in water, loosely covered with a bag
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat. The flavor fades as they yellow, so use them cooked, soon.
rescue: Stir them into soups, sauces or a green chimichurri

failures.title: Slimy, dark leaves
failures.symptom: Leaves, especially cilantro, turn dark green, wet and slimy inside the bag.
failures.why: Tender herbs rot quickly when wet leaves are trapped in a sealed bag, and mold is a common reason cilantro gets thrown out.
prevent: Don't wash herbs until you use them
Keep leaves dry. Only the stems should touch water
failures.verdictNote: Pick out and toss the slimy sprigs. If the whole bunch smells off, toss it.

failures.title: Wilted, droopy herbs
failures.symptom: Leaves and stems flop but are still green.
failures.why: Herbs lose water quickly, especially when they sit out or stay uncovered in the fridge.
prevent: Store tender herbs like flowers, stems in water
Wrap hardy herbs (rosemary, thyme) in a damp paper towel inside a bag
failures.verdictNote: Still good. Trim the stems and put them in cold water for 30 minutes.
rescue: Freeze chopped herbs in olive oil in an ice-cube tray

items.name: Mushroom
items.intro: Mushrooms don't care about ethylene. They fail from moisture, bruising and age, so how you package them matters most.

failures.title: Slimy, sticky surface
failures.symptom: Caps feel slick or sticky, look darker, and may smell sour or fishy.
failures.why: Plastic traps moisture, and wet mushrooms are an easy home for spoilage bacteria. Warm temperatures and long storage make it worse.
prevent: Store them in a paper bag, not plastic
Keep them dry, and clean them with a damp cloth just before cooking
failures.verdictNote: Toss mushrooms that are slimy, sticky or smell sour.

failures.title: Brown spots or darkening
failures.symptom: Caps get brown patches or darken overall, but they're still dry and firm.
failures.why: Mushrooms bruise easily, and handling makes them brown. UC Davis notes that most mushroom losses come from bruising, rough handling and age, not disease.
prevent: Handle them gently and don't stack heavy things on top
failures.verdictNote: Still good if they're dry and smell normal. Cook them.
rescue: Chop them fine into duxelles for toast, eggs or pasta

failures.title: Caps opening, gills showing
failures.symptom: The edge of the cap pulls away from the stem and the dark gills show.
failures.why: Mushrooms keep growing after harvest, so the caps open and the veil breaks over time.
prevent: Use them within about a week
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat, with a stronger flavor. Cook them soon.
rescue: Use them in soup, gravy or a mushroom sauce

failures.title: Dry, wrinkled mushrooms
failures.symptom: Mushrooms shrink, wrinkle and feel leathery.
failures.why: Mushrooms are mostly water. Left uncovered or in a paper bag for too long, they dry out.
prevent: Fold the paper bag closed
Use them within about a week
failures.verdictNote: Safe if there's no slime or mold. They work well cooked.
rescue: Slice them into soups and sauces
Dry them the rest of the way in a low oven and grind them into mushroom powder

items.name: Bell Pepper
items.intro: Peppers barely react to ethylene. They wrinkle as they lose water, get pitted if they're too cold for too long, and eventually mold.

failures.title: Soft, wrinkled skin
failures.symptom: The skin wrinkles and the walls feel soft instead of crisp.
failures.why: Peppers soften as they lose water, and red, yellow and orange peppers do it faster than green ones.
prevent: Store them whole and unwashed in the crisper drawer
Use colored peppers before green ones
failures.verdictNote: Safe if there's no mold. Wrinkled peppers are great cooked.
rescue: Roast them and blend into a sauce or dip
Slice them into fajitas or a stir-fry

failures.title: Pitting or watery patches
failures.symptom: Small sunken pits or water-soaked areas on the skin, sometimes with rot at the stem.
failures.why: Peppers kept at 41°F can show cold damage after about two weeks. Green peppers are more sensitive than colored ones.
prevent: Use peppers within one to two weeks
Keep them out of the coldest spot in the fridge
failures.verdictNote: Cut away the pitted spots and use the rest soon. Toss it if it's soft and rotting.
rescue: Dice it into salsa, eggs or chili

failures.title: Mold spot on the skin or stem
failures.symptom: Gray or black fuzz, usually near the stem or on a damaged spot.
failures.why: Gray mold grows well even at fridge temperatures, and it gets in through cuts and punctures.
prevent: Store cut peppers in an airtight container and use them within a few days
failures.verdictNote: Bell peppers are firm, so USDA says a small mold spot can be cut off with at least an inch around and below it. If there's mold inside the seed cavity or it covers more than a small spot, toss it.

items.name: Tomato
items.intro: Tomatoes are damaged by cold, keep ripening on the counter, and mold quickly once the skin splits. They also give off ethylene that hurts nearby greens.

failures.title: Mealy, bland tomatoes
failures.symptom: Flesh is soft and grainy, flavor is flat, and color may be blotchy.
failures.why: Tomatoes are damaged by cold. Below 50°F for more than two weeks, or at 41°F for more than six to eight days, they lose flavor, soften early, ripen unevenly and rot more easily.
prevent: Ripen and keep tomatoes on the counter, stem-side down
Move only fully ripe ones to the fridge, and only for a few days
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat. The texture won't come back, so cook them.
rescue: Simmer them into sauce or soup
Roast them with olive oil and garlic

failures.title: Very soft and wrinkly
failures.symptom: Tomatoes feel soft all over and the skin starts to wrinkle.
failures.why: Tomatoes keep ripening on the counter, driven by their own ethylene, until they go past their best.
prevent: Buy a mix of ripe and less-ripe tomatoes
Move fully ripe tomatoes to the fridge for a couple of days if you need more time
failures.verdictNote: Safe if there's no mold or leaking. Ideal for cooking.
rescue: Blend them into sauce, salsa or gazpacho
Save cores and skins in a freezer stock bag

failures.title: Moldy, split or leaking
failures.symptom: Fuzzy mold, a cracked skin with wet flesh, or a sour smell.
failures.why: Several molds, including gray mold and black mold, attack tomatoes, often through cracks and damaged skin.
prevent: Use split tomatoes the same day
Keep tomatoes in a single layer so they don't crush each other
failures.verdictNote: Toss it. USDA lists tomatoes as soft produce, where mold can spread below the surface.

items.name: Avocado
items.intro: Avocados have a short window. They go from ripe to overripe fast, brown inside if chilled too early, and turn rancid when rot sets in.

failures.title: Mushy and overripe
failures.symptom: The fruit gives too easily when pressed, and the flesh is very soft.
failures.why: Avocados ripen after harvest, and their own ethylene speeds up sharply as they ripen. At room temperature they can go from ripe to overripe in a day or two.
prevent: Move ripe avocados into the fridge to slow them down
Keep unripe ones on the counter, away from bananas if you don't want them to speed up
failures.verdictNote: Still good if the flesh is green and smells fresh.
rescue: Make guacamole or avocado toast
Blend it into a smoothie or salad dressing

failures.title: Brown streaks or gray flesh
failures.symptom: Brown threads or gray patches in the flesh, or a fruit that never ripens properly.
failures.why: Unripe avocados kept cold for too long get internal browning and may never ripen. Avocados should go in the fridge only once they're ripe.
prevent: Ripen avocados on the counter first, then refrigerate
failures.verdictNote: Cut away the brown parts. The rest is fine if it smells and tastes normal.
rescue: Mash the good part with lime and salt

failures.title: Black, stringy, sour or moldy
failures.symptom: Dark rot spreading from the stem or from black spots on the skin, with a sour or rancid smell.
failures.why: Fungal rots such as anthracnose and stem-end rot spread into the flesh, browning it and giving it a rancid flavor.
prevent: Eat ripe avocados within a few days
Check the stem end when buying. Green underneath is good, brown isn't
failures.verdictNote: Toss it if it smells sour or has visible mold. Avocados are soft fruit, so cutting around mold isn't safe.

items.name: Banana
items.intro: Most banana problems look worse than they are. A dark peel usually means cold or ripeness, not spoilage.

failures.title: Peel turns brown or black in the fridge
failures.symptom: The peel goes dull, gray or dark brown after time in the fridge, while the fruit inside stays pale.
failures.why: Bananas are tropical and are damaged below about 56°F. The peel discolors and unripe bananas may stop ripening.
prevent: Keep bananas on the counter
Refrigerate them only once they're fully ripe
failures.verdictNote: Still good if the banana was ripe when it went in. The peel looks bad, but the fruit is fine.

failures.title: Covered in brown spots
failures.symptom: Lots of brown speckles, with soft, sweet flesh.
failures.why: Bananas keep ripening on the counter, driven by their own ethylene, and they ripen faster when it's warm.
prevent: Separate bananas from the bunch
Keep them away from other fruit
failures.verdictNote: Still good, and at their sweetest for baking.
rescue: Peel and freeze them for smoothies or banana bread
Mash them into pancakes or oatmeal

failures.title: Brown, mushy patches inside
failures.symptom: The peel looks fine, but the flesh has brown, soft spots.
failures.why: A drop or bump can brown the flesh without breaking the peel.
prevent: Hang bananas or set them down gently
failures.verdictNote: Cut out the bruised part and eat the rest.
rescue: Use bruised bananas in baking or smoothies

failures.title: Mold on the stem or crown
failures.symptom: White, gray or black fuzz where the bananas join together.
failures.why: Crown rot, a fungal infection of the cut stem where the bunch was separated, is one of the main ways bananas spoil.
prevent: Check the crown when buying
Use bananas with a moldy crown first
failures.verdictNote: If the mold is only on the stem and the fruit is firm and smells normal, cut off the stem end and eat it. If the fruit is leaking, smells fermented or has mold on it, toss it.

items.name: Strawberry
items.intro: Mold is the number one reason strawberries get thrown out. Ethylene barely matters for them, but keeping them dry and cold does.

failures.title: Gray, fuzzy mold
failures.symptom: Gray fuzz, often starting on one berry and spreading to the ones touching it.
failures.why: Gray mold (Botrytis) causes the most strawberry losses after harvest. It grows even at 32°F, just very slowly, and moisture on the berries helps it spread.
prevent: Don't wash berries until you eat them
Store them in a single layer on paper towels
Pull out moldy berries as soon as you see them
failures.verdictNote: Toss moldy berries. Check the ones that were touching them, and toss any that are soft or wet. Strawberries are soft fruit, so you can't cut mold away.

failures.title: Soft, mushy or leaking
failures.symptom: Berries collapse, leak juice and stain the container, with no visible mold.
failures.why: Crushed berries break down fast, and Rhizopus rot causes mushy, leaky berries. It doesn't grow below 41°F, so keeping them cold helps.
prevent: Keep them in the coldest part of the fridge
Don't stack heavy things on the container
failures.verdictNote: Safe if there's no mold. Cook or blend them today.
rescue: Cook them into a quick compote or jam
Freeze them for smoothies

failures.title: Dull, shriveled berries
failures.symptom: Berries lose their shine and start to shrivel.
failures.why: Strawberries lose water through their thin skin, especially when the stems are pulled off or they're left uncovered.
prevent: Keep the green tops on until you eat them
Keep them covered in the fridge
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat. The texture is better in cooking or blended.
rescue: Roast them with a little sugar
Blend them into a smoothie

items.name: Raspberry
items.intro: Raspberries are among the most perishable fruits you can buy, lasting only two to five days even at 32°F. Mold is almost always what ends them.

failures.title: Gray, fuzzy mold
failures.symptom: Gray fuzz on a few berries, spreading through the container.
failures.why: Diseases cause most raspberry losses, and gray mold (Botrytis) is the main one. It keeps growing slowly even at 32°F.
prevent: Keep them dry and unwashed until you eat them
Store them in a single layer on a paper towel, in the coldest part of the fridge
Plan to eat them within two days
failures.verdictNote: Toss moldy berries and any soft or wet ones touching them. You can't cut mold out of soft fruit.

failures.title: Leaking, collapsing berries
failures.symptom: Berries lose their shape, leak juice and stick to each other, with no mold.
failures.why: Raspberries are hollow and fragile, and they soften quickly after harvest. Crushing speeds it up.
prevent: Don't stack containers
Handle them as little as possible
failures.verdictNote: Safe if there's no mold. Use them today.
rescue: Cook them into a quick sauce
Freeze them for smoothies

failures.title: Berries turning dark purple-red
failures.symptom: Red raspberries darken toward purple.
failures.why: Ethylene can darken red raspberries to purple-red, and it can also speed up gray mold. Raspberries are too short-lived for a Krisp to make a real difference, so the fix is to keep them away from fruit and eat them fast.
prevent: Keep raspberries away from apples, bananas and other ripening fruit
failures.verdictNote: Still good if there's no mold. The color change is cosmetic.

items.name: Apple
items.intro: Apples keep for weeks in the fridge, so most of their problems are slow ones. They go soft and mealy, wrinkle as they dry out, or rot where they were bruised. They are also the biggest ethylene source in most kitchens.

failures.title: Soft, mealy flesh
failures.symptom: The flesh is soft and grainy instead of crisp and juicy.
failures.why: Apples keep ripening after harvest, driven by their own ethylene, and they lose firmness as they go. Warmth speeds it up. UC Davis recommends storing Gala apples at about 32°F.
prevent: Keep apples in the fridge, not in a fruit bowl
Buy only what you'll eat in a few weeks
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there's no mold or rot. Mealy apples are better cooked.
rescue: Cook them into applesauce or apple butter
Bake them into a crisp, muffins or oatmeal

failures.title: Wrinkled, leathery skin
failures.symptom: The skin puckers and the apple feels lighter and slightly rubbery.
failures.why: Apples lose water slowly through the skin. They keep best at 90 to 95 percent humidity, and an open fridge shelf is much drier than that.
prevent: Keep them in the crisper drawer, in a bag with a few holes in it
failures.verdictNote: Still good. The flesh is a little less juicy, and that's all.
rescue: Slice them thin and dry them into apple chips
Chop them into oatmeal or a salad

failures.title: Brown, soft bruises
failures.symptom: Flat brown spots under the skin that feel soft when pressed.
failures.why: A bump breaks cells under the skin, and the damaged flesh browns. Wounds are also where decay gets in during storage.
prevent: Don't drop apples into the bag or the drawer
Eat bruised apples first
failures.verdictNote: Cut the bruise out and eat the rest. FDA advises cutting away damaged or bruised areas before eating.
rescue: Chop the good parts into a pie, a crisp or applesauce

failures.title: Soft brown rot or mold
failures.symptom: A soft, watery brown patch that keeps growing, sometimes with blue-green or gray fuzz.
failures.why: Blue mold and gray mold both cause decay in stored apples. Wounds are a common way in.
prevent: Check the bag every week or so and pull out damaged apples
Keep bruised or cut apples apart from sound ones
failures.verdictNote: Toss an apple that is moldy or rotting. USDA notes that mold toxins are known to occur on apples, and that mold reaches deeper than the part you can see. Check the apples that were touching it.

items.name: Blueberry
items.intro: Blueberries last longer than most berries, a week or two in the fridge. Mold is what usually ends them, followed by shriveling.

failures.title: Gray or white fuzzy mold
failures.symptom: Fuzz on a few berries, often where they touch each other or at the stem scar.
failures.why: Gray mold and Rhizopus rot are the main diseases of blueberries after harvest. Moisture on the berries helps both along.
prevent: Keep berries dry and unwashed until you eat them
Pick through the container when you get home and remove soft or damaged berries
Store them in the coldest part of the fridge
failures.verdictNote: Toss moldy berries and any soft or wet ones touching them. You can't cut mold out of soft fruit.

failures.title: Wrinkled, shriveled berries
failures.symptom: Berries lose their shine, wrinkle and feel soft.
failures.why: Water loss makes blueberries shrivel and lose their gloss. It happens faster in an open container or in dry fridge air.
prevent: Keep them covered in the fridge
Eat them within a week or two
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there's no mold. The texture is better cooked or blended.
rescue: Bake them into muffins or pancakes
Freeze them for smoothies

failures.title: Soft, leaking berries
failures.symptom: Berries turn mushy and leak juice that stains the container, with no fuzz.
failures.why: UC Davis calls these leakers: berries that break down inside as they age and leak juice.
prevent: Don't stack anything on the container
Line the container with a paper towel to catch juice
failures.verdictNote: Soft berries with no mold and no sour smell are fine cooked or frozen today. Toss any that smell fermented or have fuzz.
rescue: Simmer them into a quick compote for yogurt or oatmeal
Freeze them for smoothies

items.name: Cantaloupe
items.intro: A whole cantaloupe ripens on the counter and gives off a lot of ethylene as it does. Most losses come from letting it go too far, from rot on the rind, or from cut melon sitting too long.

failures.title: Soft, mushy flesh
failures.symptom: The melon gives easily all over, and the flesh is very soft and wet.
failures.why: Cantaloupe keeps ripening after harvest and makes a lot of its own ethylene, so going overripe is the usual problem.
prevent: Move it to the fridge as soon as the stem end smells sweet
Eat it within five to seven days of ripening
failures.verdictNote: Safe if it smells sweet. Use it today. If it smells sour or boozy, or the flesh is slimy, toss it.
rescue: Blend it into a smoothie or agua fresca
Freeze cubes for smoothies

failures.title: Mold or sunken soft spots on the rind
failures.symptom: Fuzzy white, green or black patches, or soft sunken spots, often at the stem end or where the melon sat.
failures.why: Several fungi cause decay and surface spots on cantaloupe rind.
prevent: Choose melons without soft spots, cracks or mold at the stem end
Keep the melon dry on the counter
failures.verdictNote: Toss a melon with mold or soft, sunken rot on the rind. FDA says to throw away produce that looks rotten, and a knife carries whatever is on the rind into the flesh.

failures.title: Cut melon turned slimy or sour
failures.symptom: Cut pieces feel slick, look glassy or dull, and smell sour or fermented.
failures.why: Once a melon is cut, the wet flesh is exposed and bacteria can grow on it. FDA notes that a knife can carry dirt and bacteria from the rind onto the flesh.
prevent: Scrub the rind under running water with a clean brush before you cut it
Refrigerate cut melon right away in a covered container
Eat cut melon within about three days
failures.verdictNote: Toss it. Don't taste cut melon that is slimy or smells off.

items.name: Cherry
items.intro: Cherries don't ripen after picking and barely react to ethylene. They fail from mold, from bruising and from drying out.

failures.title: Brown soft spots or fuzzy mold
failures.symptom: A soft brown spot that spreads, or gray or white fuzz, often starting near the stem or at a split.
failures.why: Brown rot, gray mold and Rhizopus rot are the main cherry diseases after harvest. Gray mold keeps growing slowly even at 32°F, and Rhizopus shows up in fruit kept at 41°F or warmer.
prevent: Keep cherries cold and dry, and don't wash them until you eat them
Pick out split or damaged cherries when you get home
failures.verdictNote: Toss moldy or rotting cherries and any soft or wet ones touching them. You can't cut mold out of soft fruit.

failures.title: Dents and soft bruises
failures.symptom: Small sunken dimples in the skin, or soft flat spots.
failures.why: Pitting is a dent left when cells under the skin collapse after an impact. Bruises come from pressure and drops.
prevent: Don't pile cherries deep or put anything on top of them
Leave the stems on until you eat them
failures.verdictNote: Still good if there's no mold or leaking. Eat the dented ones first.
rescue: Pit and freeze them for smoothies
Simmer them into a quick sauce

failures.title: Shriveled fruit and dry, brown stems
failures.symptom: The skin wrinkles, the fruit softens, and the stems turn brown and brittle.
failures.why: Cherries lose water in dry air. UC Davis lists shriveling as a quality defect and recommends 90 to 95 percent humidity.
prevent: Keep them in a bag or covered container in the fridge
failures.verdictNote: Still good. They are a little less juicy.
rescue: Pit and bake them into a clafoutis or a crisp

items.name: Grape
items.intro: Grapes don't ripen after harvest and barely react to ethylene. They last one to three weeks cold, and usually end by drying out, dropping off the stem or growing gray mold.

failures.title: Brown, slipping skins and gray fuzz
failures.symptom: Grapes turn brown, the skin slips off easily, and white threads or gray fuzz appear, usually in one part of the bunch.
failures.why: This is gray mold, the main disease of stored grapes. It moves through a bunch quickly once it starts.
prevent: Keep grapes cold and dry in their vented bag
Don't wash them until you eat them
Snip off damaged or moldy clusters as soon as you see them
failures.verdictNote: Toss moldy grapes and the ones touching them. You can't cut mold out of soft fruit.

failures.title: Grapes falling off the stem
failures.symptom: Loose grapes collect at the bottom of the bag.
failures.why: This is called shatter. It increases as grapes mature and with rough handling.
prevent: Handle the bag gently
Eat grapes within one to three weeks
failures.verdictNote: Still good if the loose grapes are firm. Rinse them and eat them first.
rescue: Freeze loose grapes as a snack
Roast them with a little oil and salt for toast or salads

failures.title: Wrinkled grapes and dry stems
failures.symptom: The stems turn brown and brittle and the grapes start to wrinkle.
failures.why: Grapes dry out in fridge air. UC Davis lists shriveled and dried berries as defects and recommends 90 to 95 percent humidity.
prevent: Keep them in their bag at the back of the fridge
Leave grapes on the stem until you eat them
failures.verdictNote: Still good if there's no mold. They taste sweeter and chewier.
rescue: Roast them or simmer them into a pan sauce

items.name: Kiwi
items.intro: Kiwi is extremely sensitive to ethylene. Ripe kiwi goes from soft to mushy quickly, especially near other ripening fruit.

failures.title: Mushy, overly soft fruit
failures.symptom: The fruit gives with almost no pressure, and the flesh is very soft and translucent.
failures.why: Kiwi softens in response to tiny amounts of ethylene. UC Davis reports that as little as 5 to 10 parts per billion is enough. Ripe kiwi also gives off plenty of its own.
prevent: Once ripe, keep kiwi in the fridge, away from apples, bananas and pears
Ripen only as many as you'll eat in a few days
failures.verdictNote: Safe if it smells fresh and there's no mold. Toss it if it smells fermented.
rescue: Blend it into a smoothie
Mash it over yogurt or oatmeal

failures.title: Dark, soft bruises
failures.symptom: A dark, wet-looking patch in the flesh under a soft spot on the skin.
failures.why: Ripe kiwi bruises easily. Wounds are also where gray mold gets in.
prevent: Store ripe kiwi in a single layer
Don't put heavier fruit on top of it
failures.verdictNote: Cut away the bruised part and eat the rest today.
rescue: Scoop the good flesh into a smoothie

failures.title: Mold or a sour, fermented smell
failures.symptom: Gray fuzz, usually at the stem end or a wound, or a fruit that smells sour or boozy.
failures.why: Gray mold is the main kiwi disease after harvest. It can invade the fruit directly or through wounds.
prevent: Eat ripe kiwi within a few days
Remove any damaged fruit from the bag
failures.verdictNote: Toss it. Kiwi is soft fruit, so mold can't be cut away.

items.name: Lemon
items.intro: Lemons keep for weeks. When they fail, it's usually one of three things: they dry out, the peel pits in the cold, or one goes moldy and the fruit around it follows.

failures.title: Hard, shrunken lemons
failures.symptom: The peel turns hard, thin and dull, and the lemon feels light.
failures.why: Lemons lose water through the peel. They keep best at 90 to 95 percent humidity, and both a fruit bowl and an open fridge shelf are drier than that.
prevent: Keep lemons in a sealed bag in the fridge
failures.verdictNote: Still good if there's no mold. There is just less juice.
rescue: Microwave it for 10 seconds, roll it, then juice it
Zest it and freeze the zest

failures.title: Soft spot, then green or blue powder
failures.symptom: A soft, watery patch on the peel that grows white fuzz, then a dusty green or blue coating.
failures.why: These are green mold and blue mold, the main diseases of citrus after harvest. They start as a water-soaked spot, then the spores appear.
prevent: Check the bag or bowl often and remove any soft lemon
Handle lemons gently. Cuts and scratches are where decay starts
failures.verdictNote: Toss a moldy lemon. Citrus is soft, juicy fruit, so mold can spread below the surface. Check the fruit that was touching it.

failures.title: Pitted or stained peel
failures.symptom: Small sunken pits or reddish-brown stains on the peel after a long stay in the fridge.
failures.why: Lemons keep best at 54 to 57°F, warmer than a fridge. After a long time in the cold the peel can pit and stain, and badly damaged fruit decays more easily.
prevent: Buy what you'll use in three to four weeks
Use the oldest lemons first
failures.verdictNote: Still good if the lemon is firm and has no mold. The damage is in the peel, so juice it.
rescue: Juice it and freeze the juice in an ice cube tray

items.name: Lime
items.intro: Limes are sensitive to cold and to ethylene. They yellow near ripening fruit, get brown leathery patches in the fridge, and dry out on the counter.

failures.title: Hard, dry limes
failures.symptom: The peel turns hard and dull and the lime gives very little juice.
failures.why: Limes lose water through the peel and keep best at 90 to 95 percent humidity. A fruit bowl is far drier than that.
prevent: Keep limes in a sealed bag in the fridge
failures.verdictNote: Still good if there's no mold. There is just less juice.
rescue: Microwave it for 10 seconds, roll it, then juice it
Zest it and mix the zest with salt

failures.title: Turning yellow
failures.symptom: The green peel fades to yellow-green, then yellow.
failures.why: Ethylene breaks down the green pigment in lime peel and lets the yellow underneath show. Apples, bananas and other ripening fruit nearby are the usual source.
prevent: Keep limes away from apples, bananas and tomatoes
Store them in a sealed bag in the fridge
failures.verdictNote: Still good if it's firm and has no mold. The change is in the peel color.

failures.title: Brown, sunken patches on the peel
failures.symptom: Small pits in the peel that merge into brown, leathery, sunken areas.
failures.why: Limes get chilling injury below 50°F, and it gets worse the colder and longer they are stored. Pits form in the peel and can merge into brown, leathery patches.
prevent: Buy limes in small amounts and use them within two to three weeks
For up to a week, the counter is fine
failures.verdictNote: Still good if the inside looks and smells normal. Juice it soon. Toss it if the patches are soft or moldy.
rescue: Juice it and freeze the juice in an ice cube tray

failures.title: Soft spot with green or blue mold
failures.symptom: A soft, watery patch that grows white fuzz and then green or blue powder.
failures.why: Green mold and blue mold are the main lime diseases after harvest, along with rots that start at the stem end. Cuts and bruises in the peel let them in.
prevent: Remove any soft lime from the bag as soon as you see it
Handle limes gently
failures.verdictNote: Toss a moldy lime. Citrus is soft, juicy fruit, so mold can spread below the surface. Check the fruit that was touching it.

items.name: Mango
items.intro: Mangoes are tropical. Chilling them before they're ripe ruins them, and once ripe they have only a few days.

failures.title: Gray, dull skin and uneven ripening
failures.symptom: Grayish, scald-like patches or pits on the skin, and fruit that ripens unevenly with poor color and flavor.
failures.why: Unripe mangoes are damaged by cold. UC Davis recommends 55°F for mature-green mangoes and 50°F for ripe ones, both well above fridge temperature. Chilled mangoes ripen unevenly, taste flat and decay more easily, and the flesh sometimes browns.
prevent: Ripen mangoes on the counter
Refrigerate only ripe mangoes, and eat them within five to seven days
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if the flesh smells fresh and has no mold. The flavor will be flat.
rescue: Blend it into a smoothie or lassi with lime
Cook it into chutney

failures.title: Black spots on the skin
failures.symptom: Dark spots that grow as the mango ripens, or a black ring around the stem.
failures.why: Anthracnose is a fungal disease that shows up as dark spots on the skin and can darken the flesh underneath. Stem-end rot starts as a round black patch around the stem.
prevent: Choose mangoes without dark sunken spots or a black stem end
Eat ripe mangoes promptly, because the spots grow as the fruit softens
failures.verdictNote: Spots that stay in the skin come off when you peel it. If the flesh underneath is dark, soft or smells off, or you see fuzzy mold, toss the mango.
rescue: Peel it, check the flesh, and cube the good fruit for the freezer

failures.title: Very soft, wrinkled or stringy
failures.symptom: The mango gives easily all over, the skin wrinkles, and the flesh is very soft.
failures.why: Mangoes keep ripening after harvest, and they give off more ethylene the warmer they are. A ripe mango on the counter goes past its best quickly.
prevent: Move ripe mangoes to the fridge
Cube and freeze ripe mango you will not eat in time
failures.verdictNote: Safe if it smells sweet and fruity. Toss it if it smells sour or like alcohol, or the flesh has turned gray or brown.
rescue: Blend it into a smoothie
Cook it down into a sauce for yogurt or ice cream

items.name: Orange
items.intro: Oranges are hardy and keep for weeks in the fridge. Mold is the main way they fail. Otherwise they slowly dry out.

failures.title: Soft spot with green or blue mold
failures.symptom: A soft, watery patch that grows white fuzz and then green or blue powder, or a sour-smelling soft rot.
failures.why: Green mold, blue mold and sour rot are among the main diseases of oranges after harvest.
prevent: Check the bag often and remove any soft orange
Don't seal oranges in an airtight bag
failures.verdictNote: Toss a moldy orange. Citrus is soft, juicy fruit, so mold can spread below the surface. Check the fruit that was touching it.

failures.title: Shriveled peel around the stem
failures.symptom: The peel around the stem end dries, sinks and turns brown, and the orange feels lighter.
failures.why: As an orange ages, the peel around the stem dries out and breaks down. UC Davis calls it stem-end rind breakdown.
prevent: Use oranges within three to four weeks
Keep them in the fridge rather than on the counter
failures.verdictNote: Still good if the fruit inside is juicy and smells fresh, with no mold.
rescue: Juice it

failures.title: Pitted or brown-stained peel
failures.symptom: Small sunken pits or brown stains on the peel after cold storage.
failures.why: Some oranges get chilling injury in the cold: pits and brown stains on the peel, and more decay afterward. How cold is too cold depends on the variety and where it was grown.
prevent: Keep oranges in the crisper drawer rather than against the cold back wall
Use them within three to four weeks
failures.verdictNote: Still good if the orange is firm and has no mold. Peel it and eat it soon.
rescue: Juice it or segment it into a salad

items.name: Peach
items.intro: Peaches have a narrow window. They turn mealy if they're refrigerated before they're ripe, bruise easily once soft, and mold fast.

failures.title: Mealy, dry or brown inside
failures.symptom: The flesh is dry and grainy instead of juicy, sometimes brown or streaked red, with little flavor.
failures.why: This is internal breakdown, a kind of chilling injury. Peaches held at 36 to 46°F are the most prone to it, and that range includes most fridges. It shows up later, when the fruit ripens, and it can start in cold storage before the fruit reaches you.
prevent: Ripen peaches on the counter first
Refrigerate only ripe peaches, and eat them within three to five days
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there's no mold. The texture won't come back, so cook them.
rescue: Bake them into a crisp or cobbler
Simmer them into jam or a sauce

failures.title: Brown, soft bruises
failures.symptom: Flat, soft, brown areas under the skin where the fruit was pressed or bumped.
failures.why: Ripe peaches bruise under very little pressure, and some varieties bruise more easily than others.
prevent: Store them in a single layer, stem side down
Don't stack ripe peaches or bag them with heavier fruit
failures.verdictNote: Cut the bruise out and eat the rest today. Toss the peach if the bruise has gone moldy or smells sour.
rescue: Slice the good parts over yogurt or into a smoothie

failures.title: Brown soft rot or fuzzy mold
failures.symptom: A soft brown spot that spreads fast, often with tan, gray or white fuzz.
failures.why: Brown rot, gray mold and Rhizopus rot are the main peach diseases after harvest.
prevent: Eat ripe peaches within a few days
Remove any rotting peach right away and check the ones next to it
failures.verdictNote: Toss it. USDA lists peaches as soft fruit, where mold can spread below the surface.

items.name: Pear
items.intro: Pears ripen from the inside out, so by the time one feels soft all over, the core is already past it. Bruising and mold are the other ways they go.

failures.title: Mushy and brown at the core
failures.symptom: The neck is very soft, and the flesh around the core is brown, wet and mushy.
failures.why: Pears ripen after harvest and make a lot of their own ethylene as they do, which keeps pushing them along. Past ripe, the flesh softens too far and breaks down.
prevent: Check the neck every day. When it gives to gentle pressure, the pear is ripe
Move ripe pears to the fridge, away from apples and bananas
failures.verdictNote: Safe if it smells sweet and there's no mold. Cut out the brown core and use the rest today.
rescue: Simmer it into pear sauce or pear butter
Bake it into muffins or a crisp

failures.title: Brown scuffs and bruises
failures.symptom: Brown marks or bands on the skin, or soft brown flesh underneath.
failures.why: Pears mark easily. Rubbing and vibration leave brown spots or bands on the skin, and an impact browns the flesh underneath.
prevent: Carry and store pears in a single layer
Handle ripe pears as little as possible
failures.verdictNote: Skin scuffs are cosmetic. Cut out any bruised flesh and eat the rest.
rescue: Slice the good parts into a salad or onto toast

failures.title: Soft rot or fuzzy mold
failures.symptom: A soft, watery brown patch, sometimes with blue-green or gray fuzz.
failures.why: Blue mold and gray mold are the main pear diseases after harvest.
prevent: Remove damaged pears from the bowl or bag
Eat ripe pears within three to five days
failures.verdictNote: Toss a pear that is moldy or rotting. Ripe pears are soft, juicy fruit, so mold can spread below the surface.

items.name: Pineapple
items.intro: Pineapple doesn't get sweeter after it's picked, so there is nothing to wait for. Left too long it ferments, and too long in a cold fridge browns the core.

failures.title: Soft, fizzy flesh that smells like alcohol
failures.symptom: Bright yellow, very soft flesh with gas pockets, and a smell of alcohol or vinegar.
failures.why: Yeasts ferment the sugar in overripe pineapple. UC Davis describes soft, bright-yellow flesh broken up by large gas cavities. The yeast gets in through wounds.
prevent: Eat pineapple within a few days of buying it
Choose one without soft spots, leaks or a fermented smell at the base
failures.verdictNote: Toss it if it smells like alcohol or vinegar, fizzes, or has soft, leaking patches.

failures.title: Brown, watery spots near the core
failures.symptom: Water-soaked brown spots in and around the core, sometimes spreading until the center is brown.
failures.why: Pineapple is damaged below 45°F, and a week or more is enough. Brown, water-soaked spots form in the core. Ripe fruit handles cold better than unripe fruit.
prevent: Keep a whole pineapple in the fridge for no more than about five days
Or keep it on the counter and eat it within a few days
failures.verdictNote: Cut away the brown, watery flesh. The rest is fine if it looks normal and smells sweet. Toss it if it smells fermented.
rescue: Grill or roast the good pieces
Freeze chunks for smoothies

failures.title: Dark, soft patches on the shell
failures.symptom: A slightly darker patch of shell that gives way under light pressure, with soft, watery flesh underneath.
failures.why: This is black rot, a fungal disease. The flesh under the patch softens, and the skin over it breaks easily.
prevent: Check the base and sides for soft spots before buying
Don't let a whole pineapple sit for more than a few days
failures.verdictNote: Toss it. FDA says to throw away produce that looks rotten.

items.name: Plum
items.intro: Plums ripen on the counter and bruise less easily than peaches. The usual problems are flesh that browns after a cold stay, fruit left too long, and mold.

failures.title: Brown, glassy or mealy flesh
failures.symptom: The flesh looks translucent or brown, tastes flat and feels mealy, even though the skin looks fine.
failures.why: This is internal breakdown, a kind of chilling injury. Plums held at 36 to 46°F are the most prone to it, and that range includes most fridges. It shows up later, as the fruit ripens.
prevent: Ripen plums on the counter until slightly soft
Refrigerate only ripe plums, and eat them within three to five days
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there's no mold. The flavor and texture are poor, so cook them.
rescue: Roast them with a little sugar
Simmer them into jam or a sauce

failures.title: Very soft and wrinkled
failures.symptom: The plum gives easily all over, and the skin wrinkles or splits.
failures.why: Plums keep ripening after harvest and make far more ethylene once ripe and warm than they do cold.
prevent: Move ripe plums to the crisper drawer
Store them in a single layer
failures.verdictNote: Safe if it smells sweet and there's no mold or leaking. Use it today.
rescue: Simmer them into a quick compote
Bake them into a cake or crumble

failures.title: Brown soft rot or fuzzy mold
failures.symptom: A soft brown spot that spreads, often with tan, gray or white fuzz.
failures.why: Brown rot, gray mold and Rhizopus rot are the main plum diseases after harvest.
prevent: Don't wash plums until you eat them
Remove any rotting plum right away
failures.verdictNote: Toss it. Plums are soft, juicy fruit, so mold can spread below the surface.

items.name: Watermelon
items.intro: Whole watermelon keeps best at cool room temperature, not in the fridge. It turns mealy around ripening fruit, loses color and flavor in the cold, and spoils quickly once cut.

failures.title: Mealy, mushy flesh
failures.symptom: The flesh is grainy and soft instead of crisp.
failures.why: Watermelon makes very little ethylene but reacts badly to it. UC Davis reports that 5 parts per million for a week at 64°F causes an unacceptable loss of firmness and eating quality. Hard knocks do something similar: internal bruising makes the flesh break down early and turn mealy.
prevent: Keep whole watermelon away from apples, bananas, peaches and other ripening fruit
Carry it and set it down gently
failures.verdictNote: Safe if it smells fresh and sweet. The texture is better blended. Toss it if it smells sour or fizzes.
rescue: Blend it into juice, agua fresca or a slushie
Freeze cubes for smoothies

failures.title: Pale, bland flesh after the fridge
failures.symptom: Small pits in the rind, with flesh that has lost some of its color and flavor.
failures.why: Whole watermelon is damaged by several days below about 45°F. The rind pits, the flesh loses color and flavor, and it decays faster once it comes back to room temperature.
prevent: Keep whole watermelon on the counter or in a cool room
Chill it for a day before serving rather than for a week
failures.verdictNote: Still good if it smells fresh. It just won't taste as sweet.
rescue: Toss it with lime, salt and chili
Blend it into a drink

failures.title: Cut watermelon turned slimy or sour
failures.symptom: Cut pieces feel slick, look dull and smell sour, or the juice fizzes.
failures.why: Cut watermelon is wet and exposed, so bacteria and yeasts can grow on it. FDA notes that a knife can carry dirt and bacteria from the rind onto the flesh.
prevent: Scrub the rind under running water before you cut it
Wrap cut watermelon tightly and refrigerate it right away
Eat cut watermelon within three to five days
failures.verdictNote: Toss it. Don't taste cut melon that is slimy, fizzy or smells off.

items.name: Nectarine
items.intro: Nectarines behave like peaches. A fridge turns unripe ones mealy, ripe ones go soft within days, and rot moves fast.

failures.title: Mealy, flavorless flesh
failures.symptom: The flesh is dry and grainy, sometimes brown or streaked red, and the fruit never gets juicy.
failures.why: Nectarines held at 36 to 46°F are prone to internal breakdown, a kind of chilling injury, and most fridges sit in that range. The damage shows when the fruit ripens: mealy or brown flesh, red bleeding and little flavor.
prevent: Ripen nectarines on the counter, stem side down
Refrigerate them only once ripe, and eat them within three to five days
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there's no mold. Cooking is the best use.
rescue: Grill or roast them
Cook them into a crisp or a jam

failures.title: Wrinkled and very soft
failures.symptom: The skin wrinkles and the fruit feels squishy all over.
failures.why: Nectarines keep ripening on the counter. Ripe fruit at room temperature gives off many times more ethylene than unripe fruit does.
prevent: Move ripe nectarines to the fridge
Keep them in a single layer
failures.verdictNote: Safe if it smells sweet and there's no mold or leaking. Use it today.
rescue: Blend them into a smoothie
Simmer them into a sauce for yogurt or pancakes

failures.title: Brown soft rot or fuzzy mold
failures.symptom: A soft brown spot that spreads quickly, often with tan, gray or white fuzz.
failures.why: Brown rot, gray mold and Rhizopus rot are the main diseases of nectarines after harvest.
prevent: Remove any rotting fruit right away and check the ones next to it
Don't wash nectarines until you eat them
failures.verdictNote: Toss it. USDA lists peaches as soft fruit, where mold can spread below the surface, and nectarines are the same.

items.name: Papaya
items.intro: Papaya is damaged below about 54°F unless it's already ripe. Chilled too early, it pits, blotches and never ripens properly. Ripe, it has only a few days.

failures.title: Blotchy skin that never ripens
failures.symptom: Pitted or blotchy skin, hard patches in the flesh, and fruit that stays partly green and bland.
failures.why: Papaya gets chilling injury below about 54°F, and green fruit is hit hardest. The skin pits and blotches, the fruit ripens unevenly, and the flesh can stay hard or turn watery. It also decays more easily.
prevent: Ripen papaya on the counter until the skin is mostly yellow
Refrigerate only ripe papaya
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if the flesh smells fresh and has no mold. It will be bland.
rescue: Blend it into a smoothie with lime
Cook green, firm papaya in a curry or stir-fry

failures.title: Brown, sunken spots on the skin
failures.symptom: Small brown, water-soaked spots that grow as the fruit ripens, or a dark stem end.
failures.why: Anthracnose is the main papaya disease after harvest. It starts as small, brown, shallow spots that can enlarge. Other fungi rot the stem end, turning it dark brown to black.
prevent: Choose papayas without sunken spots or a dark, soft stem end
Eat ripe papaya promptly
failures.verdictNote: Shallow spots that stay in the skin come off when you peel it. If the flesh underneath is soft, dark or smells off, or you see fuzzy mold, toss the papaya.
rescue: Peel it, check the flesh, and cube the good fruit for the freezer

failures.title: Mushy, very soft flesh
failures.symptom: The fruit gives easily all over and the flesh is very soft.
failures.why: Papaya keeps ripening after harvest, softening and yellowing as it goes, and it does so faster when warm.
prevent: Move ripe papaya to the fridge
Store cut papaya in a covered container and eat it within a few days
failures.verdictNote: Safe if it smells sweet. Toss it if it smells sour or fermented, or the flesh is slimy.
rescue: Blend it into a smoothie
Freeze cubes for later

items.name: Pomegranate
items.intro: Pomegranates keep for a month or more in the fridge and don't ripen after harvest. They mostly dry out. The thing to watch for is rot inside, which the skin can hide.

failures.title: Hard, shrunken, leathery skin
failures.symptom: The skin dries, hardens and pulls in around the arils.
failures.why: Pomegranates are very prone to water loss, which shrivels the skin.
prevent: Keep whole pomegranates in the fridge, in a bag
failures.verdictNote: Usually still good. Open it: if the arils are plump and smell fresh, eat them.
rescue: Freeze the arils in a single layer
Juice them

failures.title: Brown or black arils inside
failures.symptom: Arils that are brown, black or mushy, sometimes with an off-color patch of skin outside.
failures.why: Heart rot is a fungal infection that blackens the arils while the outside looks close to normal. Gray mold works from the outside in: the rind turns light brown and leathery, then gray fuzz appears.
prevent: Choose fruit that feels heavy, with no soft or discolored patches
Refrigerate pomegranates rather than leaving them out for weeks
failures.verdictNote: Toss it if the arils are black, mushy or moldy, or smell fermented.

failures.title: Brown patches on the skin
failures.symptom: Brown discoloration on the skin after a long time in cold storage.
failures.why: After two months or more in the cold, pomegranate skin can turn brown. UC Davis describes husk scald, which stays in the skin, and chilling injury, which can also leave the arils pale and the white membranes brown.
prevent: Use pomegranates within a month or two
Eat the oldest ones first
failures.verdictNote: Still good if the arils inside are firm, juicy and smell fresh, with no mold.
rescue: Scatter the arils over salads or yogurt

items.name: Asparagus
items.intro: Asparagus keeps growing after it's cut, which is why it goes downhill so fast. The spears turn woody, go limp, or get slimy at the tips, usually within a week.

failures.title: Tough, woody spears
failures.symptom: Spears are tough and stringy, especially toward the cut end.
failures.why: Asparagus builds woody fiber after harvest. UC Davis notes that ethylene speeds this toughening up, and that includes the ethylene bruised spears make themselves.
prevent: Keep asparagus away from apples, avocados and peaches
Handle the bunch gently
Cook it within three to five days
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat. Snap or cut off the tough ends and peel the lower stalks.
rescue: Peel the lower stalks and roast or grill them
Simmer the tough ends into soup and blend it

failures.title: Limp, bendy spears
failures.symptom: Spears bend instead of snapping, and the cut ends look dry and shrunken.
failures.why: Asparagus dries out fast. UC Davis recommends 95 to 100 percent humidity and counts dried-out ends as a quality defect.
prevent: Stand the bunch upright in a jar with an inch of water and cover it loosely with a bag
Or wrap the cut ends in a damp paper towel
failures.verdictNote: Still good if the tips aren't slimy and it smells fresh.
rescue: Trim the ends and stand the spears in cold water for an hour
Roast or sauté them

failures.title: Dark, slimy tips
failures.symptom: The tips turn dark, mushy and slimy, and smell bad.
failures.why: This is bacterial soft rot. UC Davis notes that it can start at the tips or at the cut end.
prevent: Keep the tips dry. Only the cut ends should sit in water
Change the water every day or two
Use asparagus within a few days
failures.verdictNote: Toss slimy or bad-smelling spears. FDA says to throw away produce that looks rotten. Check the rest of the bunch, and cook any firm, fresh-smelling spears today.

failures.title: Tips opening up
failures.symptom: The tight tips loosen and spread open, and the spears bend upward.
failures.why: Asparagus keeps growing after it's cut. The tips open up, which growers call feathering, and the spears bend away from gravity. It happens quickly above 50°F.
prevent: Refrigerate asparagus as soon as you get home
Store it upright
failures.verdictNote: Still good. It's a sign of age, so cook it soon.
rescue: Roast, grill or sauté it

items.name: Brussels Sprouts
items.intro: Brussels sprouts are very sensitive to ethylene. The outer leaves yellow and fall off first, then the sprouts go limp, and old or bruised ones turn dark and slimy.

failures.title: Yellow, loose outer leaves
failures.symptom: The outer leaves turn yellow and come away from the sprout.
failures.why: Ethylene makes Brussels sprouts yellow and shed their outer leaves. They make little of it themselves, so the source is usually ripening fruit nearby.
prevent: Keep them away from apples, pears and tomatoes
Store them in a breathable bag in the crisper drawer
failures.verdictNote: Peel off the yellow leaves. The sprout underneath is fine if it's firm and green.
rescue: Roast them
Shred them for a slaw or a quick sauté

failures.title: Soft, limp sprouts
failures.symptom: Sprouts feel soft and loose instead of tight and firm.
failures.why: Without high humidity, sprouts lose water and go limp. UC Davis recommends above 95 percent humidity.
prevent: Keep them in a bag in the crisper drawer
Buy them on the stalk when you can
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there's no slime or bad smell.
rescue: Roast them at high heat
Shred and sauté them

failures.title: Dark, slimy leaves
failures.symptom: Dark, wet, slimy leaves and a strong bad smell.
failures.why: This is bacterial soft rot. It usually follows bruising or other damage.
prevent: Don't wash them until you cook them
Use them within three to five days
failures.verdictNote: Toss sprouts that are slimy or smell bad. FDA says to throw away produce that looks rotten. Sort the rest and cook the firm ones soon.

items.name: Cabbage
items.intro: Cabbage is one of the longest-keeping vegetables, a month or two in the fridge. The outer leaves take the damage: they yellow around ethylene, speckle with age, and brown where the head was cut.

failures.title: Yellow, loose outer leaves
failures.symptom: The outer leaves turn yellow and separate from the head.
failures.why: Ethylene makes cabbage leaves yellow and detach. Cabbage makes very little of it, so the source is usually fruit stored nearby.
prevent: Keep cabbage away from apples, avocados and peaches
Store it whole in the crisper drawer
failures.verdictNote: Peel off the yellow leaves. The head underneath is fine if it's firm and crisp.
rescue: Shred it for slaw
Sauté or braise it

failures.title: Small black specks on the leaves
failures.symptom: Tiny dark specks on the ribs and veins of the leaves, like ground pepper.
failures.why: This is pepper spot, also called black leaf speck. It's a storage disorder, not mold. It's tied to cold weather in the field and late harvest, and it develops further when cabbage goes from cold storage to warmer temperatures.
prevent: Choose heads without specks on the outer leaves
Keep cabbage in the fridge rather than letting it sit out
failures.verdictNote: Still good. The specks are cosmetic. Peel off the outer leaves if they bother you.
rescue: Use it cooked, where the specks disappear

failures.title: Gray or brown cut edge
failures.symptom: The cut face of a half head turns gray-brown or black.
failures.why: Cut and broken cabbage tissue browns. UC Davis notes that broken ribs brown and decay more easily too.
prevent: Don't cut the head until you need it
Wrap the cut face tightly
Peel off whole leaves when you only need a little
failures.verdictNote: Shave off the discolored layer. The cabbage underneath is fine if it's crisp and smells fresh.
rescue: Shred the rest for slaw or a stir-fry

failures.title: Slimy or moldy outer leaves
failures.symptom: Dark, slimy, bad-smelling leaves, or gray fuzz on the outside of the head.
failures.why: Bacterial soft rot breaks leaves down into slime. Gray mold and other fungi also attack stored cabbage.
prevent: Keep the head dry and unwashed until you use it
Check stored cabbage every week or two and peel off any leaves that are going
failures.verdictNote: Cabbage is firm, so USDA says a small mold spot can be cut off with at least an inch around and below it. Peel away the affected outer leaves as well. If the slime or smell reaches into the head, toss it.
rescue: Cook what is left the same day

items.name: Cauliflower
items.intro: Cauliflower shows every problem on its white head. It discolors around ethylene, browns where it was bumped, and grows dark spots as it ages.

failures.title: Discolored head and yellow leaves
failures.symptom: The white head turns dull or yellowish-brown, and the green leaves yellow and drop off.
failures.why: UC Davis notes that even low levels of ethylene discolor the head and make the outer leaves yellow and detach.
prevent: Keep it away from apples, pears and tomatoes
Store it in a loose bag in the crisper drawer
failures.verdictNote: Trim any discolored surface and pull off the yellow leaves. The rest is fine if it's firm and smells fresh.
rescue: Roast it
Rice it or blend it into soup

failures.title: Brown, bruised patches
failures.symptom: Brown patches where the head was pressed or bumped.
failures.why: Bruised cauliflower browns quickly and decays sooner.
prevent: Store it stem side up, so the head isn't resting on the shelf
Don't stack anything on it
failures.verdictNote: Shave or cut off the brown patches. The rest is still good.
rescue: Roast or steam the rest

failures.title: Dark spots, fuzz or slime
failures.symptom: Small dark spots on the head that spread, sometimes gray fuzz, or soft, slimy, bad-smelling patches.
failures.why: Black spot and gray mold are fungal. Bacterial soft rot turns the head soft and slimy. All of them get more likely after three to four weeks of storage, or sooner if the cauliflower is kept too warm.
prevent: Don't wash it until you cook it
Use it within one to two weeks
failures.verdictNote: Cauliflower is firm, so USDA's rule for firm vegetables applies: cut off small mold spots with at least an inch around and below them. If the spots are widespread, or the head is soft, slimy or smells bad, toss it.
rescue: Cook the trimmed head the same day

items.name: Corn
items.intro: Sweet corn is at its best the day it's picked. After that the sugar turns to starch, the husks dry out, and old ears mold. Eat it within a day or three.

failures.title: Starchy, bland kernels
failures.symptom: The kernels are tough and doughy, and the corn isn't sweet.
failures.why: Corn turns its sugar into starch after harvest. UC Davis says standard sweet corn isn't stored for more than a few days because quality drops quickly, even at ideal temperatures. Warmth makes it faster.
prevent: Refrigerate corn as soon as you get home
Eat it within one to three days
Keep it in the husk until you cook it
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there's no mold, slime or sour smell. It just isn't sweet.
rescue: Cut the kernels off for chowder, cornbread or fritters
Sauté the kernels with butter and salt

failures.title: Dry, papery husks
failures.symptom: The husks turn pale, dry and papery, and the silk dries out.
failures.why: Corn loses moisture after picking. UC Davis notes that the stalk ends are trimmed short to limit it.
prevent: Keep the husks on
Store the ears in a bag in the crisper drawer
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if the kernels look normal and there's no mold or sour smell. The ear is past its best.
rescue: Cut the kernels off and add them to soup or a stir-fry

failures.title: Mold, slime or a sour smell
failures.symptom: Fuzzy mold on the silk or the tip of the ear, or kernels that are slimy or smell sour.
failures.why: UC Davis notes that the dry silk often grows surface mold once corn has been stored for more than about 10 days. Corn that old is well past its best.
prevent: Buy corn close to when you plan to eat it
Keep it cold and dry
failures.verdictNote: Toss an ear with mold, slime or a sour smell. Corn kernels are soft and moist, so mold can spread below the surface.

items.name: Eggplant
items.intro: Eggplant is a warm-weather crop that doesn't like the fridge. It pits and browns in the cold, wrinkles as it dries out, and browns at the cap around ethylene. Use it within a few days.

failures.title: Pitted skin and brown seeds
failures.symptom: Pits and bronze patches on the skin, with brown seeds and flesh inside.
failures.why: Eggplant is damaged below 50°F. At 41°F the injury shows in six to eight days, and it adds up over time. Most fridges run around 37°F to 40°F.
prevent: Use eggplant within a few days of buying it
Keep it in the warmest part of the fridge
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if it's firm and smells fresh, with no mold. Cut away any badly browned flesh and cook it soon.
rescue: Roast it and blend it into a dip
Cook it into a curry or stew

failures.title: Wrinkled skin and spongy flesh
failures.symptom: The skin loses its shine and wrinkles, and the flesh feels spongy.
failures.why: These are the signs of water loss. UC Davis notes that long, thin Japanese eggplants lose water three times faster than the large globe type.
prevent: Use it within five to seven days
Keep it in the crisper drawer
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there's no mold or soft rot. The texture is better cooked down.
rescue: Roast it and mash it into a dip
Dice it into a pasta sauce

failures.title: Brown cap and early browning
failures.symptom: The green cap turns brown and may come loose, and the eggplant browns sooner than it should.
failures.why: Above about 1 part per million, ethylene can make the cap drop off and speeds up deterioration, browning in particular.
prevent: Keep it away from apples, bananas and tomatoes
Use it within a few days
failures.verdictNote: Still good if the eggplant is firm and the flesh looks normal. Cut off the cap and cook it soon.
rescue: Slice and roast or grill it

failures.title: Soft, sunken spots or mold
failures.symptom: Soft, sunken, dark patches, or gray, black or white fuzz.
failures.why: Several molds rot eggplant, including gray mold, black mold and Rhizopus. Eggplant also bruises easily when it's stacked or handled roughly.
prevent: Don't stack anything on it
Don't wash it until you cook it
failures.verdictNote: Toss it. Eggplant flesh is soft and spongy, so mold can spread below the surface.

items.name: Garlic
items.intro: Garlic keeps for months in a dry pantry. When it goes, it sprouts, dries out into shrunken cloves, or turns soft and moldy.

failures.title: Green shoots
failures.symptom: A green shoot grows from the top of the clove, or shows in the center when you cut it.
failures.why: Sprouting means the garlic has come out of dormancy. It happens fastest between about 40 and 65°F, cooler than a kitchen and close to fridge temperature.
prevent: Keep whole bulbs in a dry, airy spot at room temperature, not in the fridge
Buy garlic in amounts you'll use within a few months
failures.verdictNote: Still okay to eat, according to Utah State University Extension. The shoot means the garlic is older and can taste bitter, so pull it out if you like.
rescue: Roast the cloves, which mellows the flavor

failures.title: Shrunken, soft cloves
failures.symptom: Cloves feel light, soft or hollow under the papery skin.
failures.why: Garlic slowly loses water. UC Davis notes that the bulbs end up soft, spongy and shriveled.
prevent: Keep bulbs whole until you need them
Once a bulb is broken open, use the cloves within about 10 days
failures.verdictNote: Use the cloves that are still firm. Toss any that are soft, brown or sticky.
rescue: Peel the firm cloves and freeze them

failures.title: Soft, moldy cloves
failures.symptom: Blue-green or gray powder on the cloves, or cloves that are soft, spongy and crumbling.
failures.why: This is Penicillium rot. A bulb can look normal outside while the cloves turn soft and spongy, then break down into a green or gray powdery mass.
prevent: Store garlic dry, with air moving around it
Don't keep it in a sealed bag or container
failures.verdictNote: Toss the bulb. Michigan State University Extension says to throw out garlic when it's soft or moldy.

items.name: Green Beans
items.intro: Green beans are fussy: too cold and they spot, too dry and they go limp, and ethylene yellows them. They are best within five to seven days.

failures.title: Yellowing and browning
failures.symptom: The pods lose their bright green and turn yellowish or brown.
failures.why: Ethylene makes green beans lose their green color and brown faster. UC Davis reports that more than 0.1 part per million cuts their shelf life at 41°F by 30 to 50 percent.
prevent: Keep them away from apples, bananas and other ripening fruit
Store them unwashed in a breathable bag in the crisper drawer
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if they aren't slimy or moldy. They are past their best raw.
rescue: Braise them with tomatoes and garlic
Add them to soup or a stir-fry

failures.title: Rusty brown spots
failures.symptom: Small rusty-brown spots on the pods, sometimes with a dull, cloudy look.
