failures.why: Green beans keep best at 41 to 45°F, a little warmer than most fridges. Rusty-brown spots are the most common sign of cold damage. Below 41°F for more than five or six days, the pods can also turn dull and pit.
prevent: Use green beans within five to seven days
Keep them in the crisper drawer, not against the cold back wall
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if the beans are firm and not slimy. Cook them soon, because cold-damaged beans decay faster.
rescue: Blanch and freeze them
Roast or sauté them

failures.title: Limp, shriveled beans
failures.symptom: The beans bend instead of snapping, and the skin wrinkles.
failures.why: Green beans lose water quickly. UC Davis notes that about 5 percent weight loss is enough to make them shrivel and go limp.
prevent: Keep them in a bag in the crisper drawer
Don't snap or trim them until you cook them
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there's no slime or mold.
rescue: Soak them in ice water for 30 minutes before cooking
Simmer them in soup or a stew

failures.title: Slimy or moldy clumps
failures.symptom: Wet, slimy patches, or white cottony fuzz holding several beans together.
failures.why: Decay starts on broken or damaged beans and spreads to the ones touching them, forming what UC Davis calls nests. Moisture on the surface makes it worse.
prevent: Keep beans dry and unwashed until you cook them
Pick out broken or damaged beans when you get home
failures.verdictNote: Toss slimy or moldy beans and the ones stuck to them. Beans are soft and moist, so mold can't be cut away. If the rest are dry, firm and smell fresh, wash and cook them today.

items.name: Onion
items.intro: Whole onions keep for a month or more in a cool, dry, dark spot. Over time they sprout, pick up black mold under the skin, or rot from the neck down.

failures.title: Green sprouts
failures.symptom: A green shoot grows from the top, and the onion feels softer than it did.
failures.why: Onions sprout once their dormancy ends. Commercial storage holds them at 32°F, and UC Davis notes that anything from 41 to 77°F favors sprouting. That covers every spot in a house, so at home it comes down to time.
prevent: Buy onions in amounts you'll use within a month or two
Keep them cool, dry and in the dark, with air around them
failures.verdictNote: Utah State University Extension says to use sprouting onions first. If the onion is firm, with no mold, slime or bad smell, cut out the shoot and any soft layers and use the rest soon. Toss it if it's mushy or smells off.
rescue: Cook it the same week. Sprouted onions keep getting softer

failures.title: Black powder under the skin
failures.symptom: Black, sooty powder on or under the papery skin, usually near the neck.
failures.why: This is black mold. It shows up as black discoloration at the neck and on the outer layers.
prevent: Store onions dry, with air around them, not in a plastic bag
Use onions with damaged or loose skins first
failures.verdictNote: Onions are firm, so USDA says small mold spots can be cut off with at least an inch around and below them. Peel off every layer that has black powder on it and rinse what is left. If the mold runs between the inner layers, or the onion is soft or smells off, toss it.
rescue: Cook the cleaned onion the same day

failures.title: Soft, smelly layers
failures.symptom: Soft, watery or slimy layers with a sour or foul smell, sometimes only on the inside or at the neck.
failures.why: Several rots do this. Bacterial soft rot is watery and foul-smelling, sour skin turns inner layers slimy and yellow-brown, and neck rot starts at the neck and moves down through the bulb.
prevent: Choose onions with tight, dry necks and no soft spots
Keep them dry
failures.verdictNote: Toss it. FDA says to throw away produce that looks rotten. Check the onions stored next to it.

items.name: Peas
items.intro: Fresh peas lose their sweetness and tenderness within days. The pods also yellow around ethylene, and old or damp ones spot and rot.

failures.title: Yellowing pods
failures.symptom: The pods fade from bright green to yellow, and the stem end turns brown.
failures.why: UC Davis notes that long exposure to even low levels of ethylene speeds up yellowing and decay in pea pods. The small leafy cap at the stem end is more sensitive than the pod.
prevent: Keep peas away from apples, bananas and other ripening fruit
Store them in a perforated bag in the crisper drawer
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there's no slime or mold. They are past their best raw.
rescue: Stir-fry them
Simmer them in soup

failures.title: Starchy, tough peas
failures.symptom: The peas taste starchy instead of sweet, and the pods are tough.
failures.why: Peas age quickly after picking. UC Davis lists yellowing, lost tenderness and starchiness as what goes wrong with time, and all of it happens faster at 41 to 50°F than at 32°F.
prevent: Refrigerate peas right away
Eat them within three to five days
Don't shell them until you cook them
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there's no slime or mold. They are better cooked.
rescue: Simmer them into pea soup
Mash them with mint and lemon

failures.title: Spotted or slimy pods
failures.symptom: Brown spots on the pods, gray or white fuzz, or soft, wet, slimy patches.
failures.why: Several fungi spot and rot pea pods, including gray mold. Bacterial soft rot is common after rough handling.
prevent: Keep peas dry and unwashed until you use them
Handle them gently
failures.verdictNote: Toss pods that are slimy or moldy. Pea pods are soft and moist, so mold can't be cut away. If the rest are dry, firm and smell fresh, wash and cook them today.

items.name: Potato
items.intro: Potatoes keep for weeks in a cool, dark pantry. Light turns them green, time makes them sprout, and one rotting potato can spoil the bag.

failures.title: Sprouts
failures.symptom: White, pink or purple sprouts growing from the eyes.
failures.why: Potatoes sprout once their dormancy ends, and a warm room brings it on sooner.
prevent: Keep potatoes cool, dark and ventilated
Buy what you'll use within a few weeks
failures.verdictNote: If the potato is still firm, cut out the sprouts and eyes and use it. University of Illinois Extension says a firm sprouted potato is fine once the sprouts are removed. If it's also shriveled or wrinkled, don't eat it.
rescue: Cut out the sprouts, peel it and cook it this week

failures.title: Green skin
failures.symptom: Green patches on or just under the skin.
failures.why: Light makes potatoes produce chlorophyll, which is the green you see. Bitter, toxic compounds called glycoalkaloids form along with it. Solanine is the best known.
prevent: Store potatoes in the dark, in a paper bag, a basket or a closed cupboard
Don't leave them out on the counter
failures.verdictNote: Cut out small green areas. NDSU Extension says that removes most of the toxin. Peel away any green skin too. If the greening is extensive, the flesh under the skin is green, or the potato tastes bitter, throw it away.
rescue: Peel and trim it, then cook it as usual

failures.title: Soft, wet, smelly potato
failures.symptom: A soft, wet or leaking potato with a strong bad smell.
failures.why: Bacterial soft rot and several fungal rots break potatoes down. Bruised, cut or skinned potatoes are the most likely to decay.
prevent: Check the bag every week or so and remove any soft potato
Keep potatoes dry and unwashed until you use them
failures.verdictNote: Toss it. FDA says to throw away produce that looks rotten. Check the potatoes that were touching it and wipe out the bin.

failures.title: Dark spots under the skin
failures.symptom: Gray, blue-black or brown patches in the flesh when you peel or cut the potato.
failures.why: This is bruising. Bruised potato tissue turns reddish, then blue-black, over one to three days.
prevent: Don't drop the bag or toss potatoes into a bin
Store them where they will not get knocked around
failures.verdictNote: Cut the dark spots out. The rest of the potato is fine if it's firm.
rescue: Trim it and cook it as usual

items.name: Sweet Potato
items.intro: Sweet potatoes are a pantry item. The fridge damages them, a warm kitchen dries them out, and broken skin lets rot in.

failures.title: Hard center after cooking
failures.symptom: Parts of the sweet potato stay hard however long it's cooked, and the flesh looks darker than usual.
failures.why: Sweet potatoes get chilling injury at 55°F or below, so a fridge damages them. UC Davis calls the result hardcore: cooked roots with a hard center and darker color. Chilled roots can also brown inside, shrivel and rot.
prevent: Keep sweet potatoes in a cool, dark pantry, not the fridge
Use them within about a month
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there's no mold, rot or off smell. Some parts may never soften.
rescue: Cut it into small cubes and simmer it in soup or stew
Mash the parts that soften

failures.title: Wrinkled, shriveled ends
failures.symptom: The ends shrivel and the skin wrinkles.
failures.why: Sweet potatoes lose water in storage. They lose it faster where the skin is scraped or broken, and faster above about 59°F.
prevent: Handle them gently. The skin is thin
Keep them away from the stove and other warm spots
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if it's still firm, with no mold or soft, wet spots. Cut off the dried ends.
rescue: Roast it
Peel, cube and simmer it in soup

failures.title: Soft, moldy or black patches
failures.symptom: Soft, wet patches, white or gray fuzz, or dark sunken spots.
failures.why: Rhizopus soft rot, black rot and Fusarium rot all attack stored sweet potatoes. Broken skin and cold damage both make decay more likely.
prevent: Use sweet potatoes with scraped or broken skin first
Don't wash them until you cook them
failures.verdictNote: Toss a sweet potato with soft, wet or moldy patches or an off smell. FDA says to throw away produce that looks rotten.

items.name: Zucchini
items.intro: Zucchini is damaged by temperatures below 41°F, and most fridges run a little colder than that. It pits and goes watery in the cold, yellows around ethylene, and turns rubbery as it dries out.

failures.title: Pitted, watery spots
failures.symptom: Small sunken, watery pits in the skin, followed by discoloration and soft spots.
failures.why: Zucchini gets chilling injury after more than a day or two below 41°F. The damage adds up over time and leads to faster decay.
prevent: Use zucchini within five to seven days
Keep it in the warmest part of the fridge
failures.verdictNote: If the zucchini is still firm, cut away the pitted spots and use it soon. If it's soft, slimy or moldy, toss it.
rescue: Grate it into fritters, muffins or zucchini bread
Sauté or roast it

failures.title: Turning yellow
failures.symptom: Dark green skin fades toward yellow.
failures.why: UC Davis notes that low levels of ethylene speed up yellowing in green summer squash.
prevent: Keep it away from apples, bananas and tomatoes
Store it in a bag in the crisper drawer
failures.verdictNote: Still good if it's firm, with no soft or slimy spots.
rescue: Sauté or roast it
Grate it into a frittata

failures.title: Rubbery, shriveled zucchini
failures.symptom: The zucchini bends, feels soft, and the skin wrinkles, usually from the ends.
failures.why: Summer squash loses water quickly after harvest, which makes it lose firmness and shrivel.
prevent: Keep it in a plastic bag in the crisper drawer
Don't wash it until you cook it
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there's no slime or mold. The texture is better cooked.
rescue: Grate it into soup, pasta sauce or baking
Roast it

failures.title: Slimy or moldy spots
failures.symptom: Soft, wet, slimy patches, or white or gray fuzz.
failures.why: Several rots attack summer squash, including bacterial rots and Rhizopus soft rot. Storage beyond about two weeks makes decay more likely.
prevent: Keep it dry
Handle it gently. Scuffs and bruises come from rough handling
failures.verdictNote: Toss it. Zucchini is soft and moist, like cucumber, which USDA lists as soft produce where mold can spread below the surface.

items.name: Radish
items.intro: Radishes keep a week or two. They go rubbery as they dry out, the tops yellow well before the roots give up, and warm storage brings on dark spots.

failures.title: Soft, rubbery radishes
failures.symptom: The radishes feel soft and bendy instead of crisp.
failures.why: Radishes go soft as they lose water. UC Davis recommends 95 to 100 percent humidity and notes that ice on top helps them keep a crisp texture.
prevent: Cut off the greens before storing
Keep the roots in a bag in the crisper drawer
failures.verdictNote: Still good if there are no dark, soft spots and they smell fresh.
rescue: Soak them in ice water for 30 minutes to an hour to firm them up
Slice and roast or sauté them

failures.title: Yellow, wilted tops
failures.symptom: The leafy tops turn yellow, wilt, and may go slimy.
failures.why: The tops age faster than the roots. UC Davis notes that they yellow with longer storage and with exposure to ethylene.
prevent: Cut the tops off when you get home and store them separately
Use the greens within a day or two
failures.verdictNote: Cut off and discard yellow or slimy tops. The roots are fine if they're firm.
rescue: Slice the roots into a salad

failures.title: Dark spots or soft rot
failures.symptom: Black or dark spots on the root, gray fuzz, or soft, watery, sunken patches.
failures.why: Bacterial black spot and other lesions develop when radishes are stored warmer than they should be. Soft rot and gray mold turn the root watery or fuzzy.
prevent: Keep radishes cold
Keep them in a bag, and dry them off if they are wet
failures.verdictNote: Toss radishes with dark soft spots, slime or mold. USDA allows cutting a small mold spot off firm vegetables with at least an inch around it, and a radish is too small for that. The firm, clean radishes in the bunch are fine.

items.name: Squash (Winter)
items.intro: Whole winter squash keeps for a month or more in a cool, dry pantry. Cold damages the rind, damaged rind lets rot in, and very old squash turns dry and stringy.

failures.title: Sunken pits in the rind
failures.symptom: Sunken pits on the rind, often followed by rot once the squash warms up.
failures.why: Winter squash gets chilling injury below about 50 to 55°F. A month at 41°F is enough. The rind pits, and the squash decays quickly after it comes out of the cold.
prevent: Keep whole squash in a cool pantry, not the fridge
Don't store it in an unheated garage or porch in cold weather
failures.verdictNote: Cut it open. If the flesh under the pits is firm and smells fresh, trim the pitted areas and cook it soon. Toss it if the flesh is soft, wet or moldy.
rescue: Roast it
Cube and freeze it

failures.title: Soft or moldy spots on the rind
failures.symptom: A soft, sunken or discolored patch on the rind, sometimes with fuzz.
failures.why: Several fungi cause storage rot in winter squash. Squash with a damaged rind or cold damage gets it first.
prevent: Keep squash from touching each other
Check stored squash every week or two, and use any with a damaged rind first
failures.verdictNote: Whole winter squash is hard and dense, so USDA's rule for firm vegetables applies: cut off a small mold spot with at least an inch around and below it. If the rot is soft and wet, has reached the seed cavity, or smells bad, toss the squash.
rescue: Cook the trimmed squash the same day

failures.title: Dry, stringy flesh
failures.symptom: The squash feels light, and the flesh is dry, stringy or pale.
failures.why: Squash slowly loses weight and texture in storage, and warm rooms speed it up.
prevent: Store squash somewhere cool and dry, with air around it
Use the oldest squash first
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there's no mold, soft rot or off smell.
rescue: Roast it and blend it into soup
Steam and mash it

items.name: Grapefruit
items.intro: Grapefruit keeps best at 54 to 57°F, warmer than a fridge. Over a long cold stay the peel pits and browns. Mold and drying out are the other ways it goes.

failures.title: Pitted, reddish-brown peel
failures.symptom: Sunken pits and reddish-brown patches on the peel after weeks in the fridge.
failures.why: Grapefruit gets chilling injury in cold storage: pitting, reddish-brown discoloration, off-flavors and more decay. How easily depends on the variety and the season.
prevent: Use refrigerated grapefruit within two to three weeks
For up to a week, the counter is fine
failures.verdictNote: Still good if the fruit is firm, smells fresh and has no mold. Toss it if the flesh is watery or tastes off.
rescue: Juice it
Broil the halves with a little sugar

failures.title: Soft spot with green or blue mold
failures.symptom: A soft, watery patch that grows white fuzz and then green or blue powder, or a sour-smelling soft rot.
failures.why: Green mold, blue mold and sour rot are among the main diseases of grapefruit after harvest.
prevent: Remove any soft grapefruit as soon as you see it
Keep the fruit dry
failures.verdictNote: Toss a moldy grapefruit. Citrus is soft, juicy fruit, so mold can spread below the surface. Check the fruit that was touching it.

failures.title: Soft, shriveled peel
failures.symptom: The peel wrinkles and softens, and the fruit feels light for its size.
failures.why: Grapefruit loses water through the peel and keeps best at 90 to 95 percent humidity.
prevent: Keep grapefruit in the crisper drawer
failures.verdictNote: Still good if there's no mold and it smells fresh. There is less juice.
rescue: Juice it

items.name: Apricot
items.intro: Apricots are fragile. They bruise at a touch once soft, turn brown and spongy after a cold stay, and rot quickly.

failures.title: Brown, spongy or gel-like flesh
failures.symptom: Watery patches in the flesh that turn brown, with a spongy or jelly-like texture and little flavor.
failures.why: UC Davis calls this gel breakdown or chilling injury. Apricots stored at 36 to 46°F, the range most fridges run in, have a short life and lose flavor.
prevent: Ripen apricots on the counter until slightly soft
Refrigerate only ripe apricots, and eat them within three to five days
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there's no mold and it smells fresh. Cook them.
rescue: Simmer them into jam or a compote
Roast them with honey

failures.title: Soft, brown bruises
failures.symptom: Flat, soft, dark areas where the fruit was pressed.
failures.why: Soft apricots bruise very easily.
prevent: Store them in a single layer
Handle ripe apricots as little as possible
failures.verdictNote: Cut the bruise out and eat the rest today. Toss the apricot if the bruise is moldy or smells sour.
rescue: Chop the good parts into oatmeal or yogurt

failures.title: Brown soft rot or fuzzy mold
failures.symptom: A soft brown spot that spreads, often with tan, gray or white fuzz.
failures.why: Brown rot and Rhizopus rot are the main apricot diseases after harvest.
prevent: Remove any rotting apricot right away
Don't wash apricots until you eat them
failures.verdictNote: Toss it. Apricots are soft, juicy fruit, so mold can spread below the surface.

items.name: Honeydew
items.intro: Honeydew is damaged by fridge temperatures unless it's already ripe. An unripe one that goes in cold may never ripen, and cut melon needs to be eaten within a few days.

failures.title: Tan or reddish patches on the rind
failures.symptom: Reddish-tan blotches or small pits on the rind after time in the fridge. The melon may stay hard and bland.
failures.why: Honeydew is damaged by several days below 45°F, and most fridges run around 37°F to 40°F. The rind pits and discolors, the melon may fail to ripen, and it picks up off-flavors and decays more easily.
prevent: Ripen whole honeydew on the counter
Refrigerate it only once it's ripe, and eat it within a few days
failures.verdictNote: Cut it open. If the flesh looks and smells normal, it's fine to eat, though it may be bland. Toss it if the rind is soft or moldy or the flesh smells off.
rescue: Blend bland melon with lime juice and a little honey
Freeze cubes for smoothies

failures.title: Mold on the rind
failures.symptom: Gray, black or pink fuzzy patches on the rind, usually underneath or at the stem end.
failures.why: Surface molds grow on honeydew when the rind stays damp. UC Davis notes that long periods of high humidity or condensation encourage them.
prevent: Keep the melon dry, and wipe off condensation when it comes out of the fridge
Don't leave it sitting in a wet spot or a sealed bag
failures.verdictNote: Toss a melon with mold or soft rot on the rind. FDA says to throw away produce that looks rotten, and a knife carries what's on the rind into the flesh.

failures.title: Cut melon turned slimy or sour
failures.symptom: Cut pieces feel slick and smell sour or fermented.
failures.why: Cut melon is wet and exposed, so bacteria can grow on it. FDA notes that a knife can carry dirt and bacteria from the rind onto the flesh.
prevent: Scrub the rind under running water with a clean brush before cutting
Wrap cut melon tightly and refrigerate it right away
Eat cut melon within a few days
failures.verdictNote: Toss it. Don't taste cut melon that is slimy or smells off.

items.name: Blackberry
items.intro: Blackberries are very perishable, good for only two to five days even at 32°F. Mold and crushing end most of them.

failures.title: Gray, fuzzy mold
failures.symptom: Gray or white fuzz that starts on one berry and spreads through the container.
failures.why: Gray mold and Rhizopus rot are the main diseases of blackberries after harvest. Moisture on the berries helps both along.
prevent: Keep them dry and unwashed until you eat them
Spread them in a single layer on a paper towel, in the coldest part of the fridge
Plan to eat them within two or three days
failures.verdictNote: Toss moldy berries and any soft or wet ones touching them. You can't cut mold out of soft fruit.

failures.title: Crushed, leaking berries
failures.symptom: Berries at the bottom lose their shape and leak dark juice, with no mold.
failures.why: Ripe blackberries are very soft. Stacked deep, the bottom layer gets crushed and leaks.
prevent: Don't stack containers or put anything on top
Handle them as little as possible
failures.verdictNote: Safe if there's no mold and no sour smell. Use them today.
rescue: Cook them into a quick sauce or jam
Freeze them for smoothies

failures.title: Dull, shriveled berries
failures.symptom: Berries lose their shine and start to wrinkle.
failures.why: Water loss makes berries shrivel and lose their gloss.
prevent: Keep them covered in the fridge
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there's no mold. The texture is better cooked or blended.
rescue: Bake them into a cobbler or muffins
Blend them into a smoothie

items.name: Jalapeño
items.intro: Jalapeños keep a week or two in the fridge. They wrinkle as they dry out, and very long cold storage pits the skin and darkens the seeds. Turning red is just ripening.

failures.title: Wrinkled, soft skin
failures.symptom: The skin wrinkles and the pepper feels soft instead of firm.
failures.why: Chiles lose firmness as they lose water. It happens faster above 45°F.
prevent: Keep them in a paper bag or loosely wrapped in the crisper drawer
Don't wash them until you use them
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there's no mold or slimy spots. Wrinkled jalapeños are fine cooked.
rescue: Roast or blister them
Pickle them, or dice and freeze them

failures.title: Pitted skin and dark seeds
failures.symptom: Small sunken pits in the skin, with seeds or the inside of the pepper turning brown.
failures.why: Chiles keep best at about 45°F. At 41°F they hold for at least two weeks without visible damage. After two to three weeks the seeds start to darken, and the skin can pit, soften and decay.
prevent: Use jalapeños within one to two weeks
Freeze them whole if you have more than you can use
failures.verdictNote: Still good if the pepper is firm, with no mold or slimy spots. Scrape out the dark seeds.
rescue: Dice and freeze them
Cook them into salsa or chili

failures.title: Turning red
failures.symptom: Green jalapeños slowly turn red, often starting in streaks.
failures.why: That's ripening, not spoilage. UC Davis notes that jalapeños don't respond to ethylene, so the fruit bowl isn't to blame. The color changes faster above 45°F.
prevent: Keep them in the fridge if you want them to stay green
failures.verdictNote: Still good. Red jalapeños are riper and a little sweeter.

failures.title: Soft spots or mold
failures.symptom: Soft, wet, sunken spots, or gray or black fuzz, often at the stem or a nick in the skin.
failures.why: Gray mold, Alternaria and bacterial soft rot attack damaged tissue. Punctures, scrapes and crushing make decay more likely.
prevent: Handle them gently
Keep them dry
failures.verdictNote: USDA lists bell peppers as firm produce, where a small mold spot can be cut off with an inch around it. A jalapeño is too small for that, so toss it.

items.name: Cranberry
items.intro: Fresh cranberries are tough for a berry and keep for weeks. Sort them before you cook: soft or brown ones go, firm ones stay.

failures.title: Soft, brown or leaking berries
failures.symptom: Some berries in the bag are soft, brown or wet, while the rest are firm.
failures.why: Cranberries can be held for two to four months in cold storage, so a bag may not be new when you buy it. Berries that break down go soft and leak, and decay follows.
prevent: Sort the bag when you get home and remove soft berries
Keep them dry and unwashed until you use them
Freeze them if you won't use them within a few weeks
failures.verdictNote: Sort them. Toss berries that are soft, brown, leaking or moldy. The firm, glossy ones are fine to use.
rescue: Cook the firm ones into sauce or bake them into bread
Freeze the firm ones in their bag

failures.title: Dull, rubbery berries
failures.symptom: Berries lose their shine and feel rubbery instead of firm.
failures.why: Cranberries are the one common berry that can get too cold. Below 37°F they can develop chilling injury: a dull look, a rubbery texture and more decay.
prevent: Keep them in the main part of the fridge, not against the back wall
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if they aren't soft, leaking or moldy. Cook them.
rescue: Simmer them into cranberry sauce

failures.title: Shriveled berries
failures.symptom: Berries wrinkle and lose their gloss.
failures.why: Water loss makes cranberries shrivel and lose their shine.
prevent: Keep them in their original bag in the fridge
failures.verdictNote: Safe if there's no mold or leaking. They are fine cooked.
rescue: Cook them into sauce, chutney or baked goods

items.name: Fig
items.intro: Fresh figs last two or three days. They sour, mold and collapse quickly, so buy them close to when you'll eat them.

failures.title: Sour or boozy smell, oozing
failures.symptom: The fig smells like alcohol or vinegar and may ooze liquid from the bottom.
failures.why: This is souring. Yeasts and bacteria ferment the fruit, and it smells of alcohol or vinegar. It usually starts before harvest, carried in by insects such as vinegar flies.
prevent: Smell figs before buying and skip any that smell sour
Refrigerate them right away
failures.verdictNote: Toss figs that smell sour or boozy, or that are oozing.

failures.title: Dark spots or fuzzy mold
failures.symptom: Small round brown or black spots, or white, pink or black fuzz, often at a split in the skin.
failures.why: Alternaria rot shows up as small, round, brown-to-black spots, and black mold as dark flesh followed by white fuzz and black spores. Cracks in the skin let them in.
prevent: Store figs in a single layer on a paper towel
Eat them within two or three days
failures.verdictNote: Toss it. Figs are soft fruit, so mold can't be cut away.

failures.title: Very soft, split or collapsing
failures.symptom: The fig slumps, the skin splits and the flesh is very soft, with no sour smell.
failures.why: Figs keep softening after harvest. Ethylene speeds up softening and decay, especially at 41°F and above.
prevent: Don't stack figs
Keep them in the coldest part of the fridge
failures.verdictNote: Safe if it smells sweet, with no sour smell, ooze or mold. Eat or cook it today.
rescue: Roast them with honey
Simmer them into a quick jam

items.name: Green Onion
items.intro: Green onions last a week or two. The tops yellow and go limp first, and bruised or wet ones turn slimy.

failures.title: Yellow tops
failures.symptom: The green tops turn yellow, starting at the tips.
failures.why: The tops yellow as they age. UC Davis notes that higher temperatures greatly speed it up.
prevent: Refrigerate green onions as soon as you get home
Use them within one to two weeks
failures.verdictNote: Cut off the yellow parts. The rest is fine if it's firm and not slimy.
rescue: Slice the good parts and freeze them
Cook them into fried rice, eggs or soup

failures.title: Limp, wilted tops
failures.symptom: The tops droop and feel soft.
failures.why: Green onions lose water quickly. UC Davis calls preventing water loss critical and recommends above 98 percent humidity.
prevent: Stand them upright in a jar with an inch of water and cover them loosely with a bag
Or wrap them in a damp paper towel inside a bag
failures.verdictNote: Still good if there's no slime or bad smell.
rescue: Trim the ends and stand them in cold water for an hour
Cook them

failures.title: Slimy leaves
failures.symptom: The leaves or outer layers turn dark, wet and slimy, and smell bad.
failures.why: This is bacterial soft rot, sometimes with gray mold. Bruising is common in green onions and leads to rapid decay.
prevent: Change the water every few days if you keep them in a jar
Don't crush the bunch under other produce
failures.verdictNote: Toss slimy or bad-smelling green onions. FDA says to throw away produce that looks rotten. Check the rest of the bunch, and use the firm, fresh-smelling ones today.

items.name: Mandarin
items.intro: Mandarins keep a week or two in the fridge. Mold is the usual ending, and one bad fruit in the bag spreads it to the rest.

failures.title: Green or blue mold
failures.symptom: A soft, wet patch turns white, then powdery green or blue.
failures.why: Green mold and blue mold are the main decay of mandarins after harvest. The spores spread from fruit to fruit and get in through small breaks in the thin peel.
prevent: Take mandarins out of the bag and check them when you get home
Refrigerate them. Cold slows mold down
Remove a moldy fruit right away
failures.verdictNote: Toss a moldy mandarin. It is a soft fruit, so mold reaches past what you can see. Firm, clean neighbors are fine after a rinse.

failures.title: Dry, shriveled fruit
failures.symptom: The peel turns leathery and loose, and the segments inside are dry.
failures.why: Mandarins have a thin peel and lose water quickly in dry air. Commercial storage holds them at 90 to 95 percent humidity, far above a fruit bowl or an open fridge shelf.
prevent: Keep them in the crisper drawer, not a bowl, if they will sit more than a few days
Eat the oldest ones first
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if it smells fine and has no mold. It will be less juicy.
rescue: Juice them
Zest the peel before it dries out completely

failures.title: Pits or brown patches on the peel
failures.symptom: Small sunken pits or brown areas show up on the peel after long cold storage.
failures.why: UC Davis lists pitting and brown discoloration as chilling injury in mandarins held below 41°F, getting worse the longer and colder they are kept, and followed by more decay. A week or two in a home fridge rarely causes it.
prevent: Eat refrigerated mandarins within about two weeks
Keep them out of the coldest spot at the back of the fridge
failures.verdictNote: Peel it. If the fruit inside looks and smells normal, it is fine. Toss it if it is soft, moldy or smells off.
rescue: Eat them soon, or juice them

items.name: Cilantro
items.intro: Cilantro lasts a week or so. Wet leaves turn to slime first, and the rest yellows and loses its flavor.

failures.title: Slimy, dark leaves
failures.symptom: Leaves turn dark green, wet and slimy inside the bag.
failures.why: Tender herbs rot quickly when wet leaves are trapped in a sealed bag. UC Davis describes bacterial soft rot as a slimy breakdown of the leaves.
prevent: Do not wash cilantro until you use it
Keep the leaves dry. Only the stems should touch water
failures.verdictNote: Pick out and toss the slimy sprigs. If the whole bunch smells off, toss it.

failures.title: Yellow leaves and faded flavor
failures.symptom: Leaves turn yellow and the bunch stops smelling like cilantro.
failures.why: Cilantro yellows as it ages, faster when it is warm. UC Davis notes its aroma drops off after about 10 days, even when the bunch still looks good enough to sell.
prevent: Keep it cold, in a jar of water with a loose bag over the top
Buy it close to when you plan to use it
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat. Pick off the yellow leaves, which have little flavor, and use the rest soon.
rescue: Blend it into salsa verde or chimichurri
Freeze chopped cilantro in oil in an ice-cube tray

failures.title: Wilted, droopy sprigs
failures.symptom: Stems and leaves flop but are still green.
failures.why: Herbs lose water quickly because they are sold in small, loose bunches. UC Davis calls water loss a serious cause of quality loss in fresh herbs.
prevent: Stand the stems in water
Cover the bunch loosely so the leaves do not dry out
failures.verdictNote: Still good. Trim the stems and stand them in cold water for 30 minutes.
rescue: Stir it into soup or rice at the end of cooking

items.name: Parsley
items.intro: Parsley is one of the longer-lasting herbs, a week or two. It yellows around ethylene and wilts when it dries out.

failures.title: Leaves turning yellow
failures.symptom: Leaves fade from deep green to yellow.
failures.why: Parsley gives off almost no ethylene but is very sensitive to it. USDA's storage handbook reports that as little as 0.4 parts per million speeds up yellowing once parsley is warmer than 32°F.
prevent: Keep the jar on a different shelf from apples, pears and tomatoes
Keep it cold
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat. Pick off the yellow leaves and use the rest soon.
rescue: Blend it into chimichurri or pesto
Add the stems to stock

failures.title: Wilted, limp sprigs
failures.symptom: Stems and leaves droop but are still green.
failures.why: USDA's storage handbook marks the end of parsley's storage life as the point where it wilts, after losing about a fifth of its weight in water.
prevent: Stand the stems in water and cover the bunch loosely
Or wrap it in a barely damp paper towel inside a bag
failures.verdictNote: Still good. Trim the stems and stand them in cold water for 30 minutes.
rescue: Chop and freeze it for cooking

failures.title: Slimy or moldy leaves
failures.symptom: Leaves turn dark and slimy, or grow gray fuzz.
failures.why: Soft-rot bacteria and gray mold both attack stored parsley. Wet leaves in a closed bag give them what they need.
prevent: Do not wash parsley until you use it
Change the water in the jar every couple of days
failures.verdictNote: Pick out and toss the slimy or moldy sprigs. If the whole bunch smells off, toss it.

items.name: Basil
items.intro: Basil is the one common herb that hates the fridge. Cold turns it black, and on the counter it wilts within a week.

failures.title: Leaves turning black
failures.symptom: Leaves get dark brown or black patches, often within a day or two of going in the fridge.
failures.why: Basil is damaged by cold, and UC Davis says to keep it above 50°F. Research has found basil leaves blacken in as little as one day at 32°F, or three days at 41°F.
prevent: Keep basil on the counter, stems in a glass of water, out of direct sun
failures.verdictNote: Cold damage isn't a safety problem, but black leaves won't recover. Pick them off and use the rest today.
rescue: Blend the good leaves into pesto and freeze it in an ice-cube tray

failures.title: Wilted, droopy leaves
failures.symptom: Leaves hang limp but are still green.
failures.why: Basil has large, thin leaves that lose water fast. UC Davis says how long it lasts depends mostly on water loss.
prevent: Stand the stems in water like cut flowers
Keep it out of direct sun and away from the stove
failures.verdictNote: Still good. Trim the stems and put them in fresh water. It often perks up within an hour.
rescue: Make pesto
Tear it into tomato sauce at the end of cooking

failures.title: Gray fuzz or slimy leaves
failures.symptom: Leaves turn dark and slimy, or grow gray fuzzy mold.
failures.why: UC Davis notes that gray mold is common on basil, and damaged or wet leaves are where it starts.
prevent: Keep the leaves dry. Only the stems should touch water
Change the water every day or two
failures.verdictNote: Pick out and toss the moldy or slimy stems. If the whole bunch smells off, toss it.

items.name: Bagged Salad
items.intro: Bagged salad is already cut and washed, so it runs on its use-by date. Once the bag is open you have about two days.

failures.title: Wet, slimy leaves
failures.symptom: Leaves turn dark, wet and slimy, and the bag smells sour.
failures.why: Cut leaves leak moisture and break down faster than a whole head. USDA's FoodKeeper gives bagged greens 3 to 5 days past the date on the bag unopened, and about 2 days once it is open.
prevent: Keep the bag cold and sealed until you need it
Tuck a dry paper towel into an opened bag or tub
Buy the bag with the latest date
failures.verdictNote: Toss the bag if the leaves are slimy or it smells sour. Picking out the bad pieces is not enough once slime has spread through the bag.

failures.title: Brown or pink cut edges
failures.symptom: The cut edges of the lettuce turn brown or pink.
failures.why: Lettuce browns where it was cut. Salad bags are packed with very little oxygen to slow this down, and it speeds up once the bag is opened.
prevent: Use an opened bag within about 2 days
Press the air out and reseal the bag between uses
failures.verdictNote: Browning on cut edges is a quality problem, not a safety one. Eat it soon if the leaves are still crisp and smell fresh.
rescue: Sauté mixed greens into eggs or pasta

items.name: Bok Choy
items.intro: Bok choy keeps about a week. The leaves yellow and wilt first, and rot starts at the base of the stalks.

failures.title: Leaves turning yellow
failures.symptom: The dark green leaves fade to yellow.
failures.why: UC Davis calls leaf yellowing the main quality problem in stored bok choy. Warm temperatures speed it up, and exposure to 5 parts per million of ethylene accelerates it.
prevent: Keep bok choy away from apples, pears and bananas
Keep it cold. It ages much faster when it is warm
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat. Trim off the yellow leaves and cook the rest soon.
rescue: Stir-fry it
Add it to soup or noodles

failures.title: Limp, wilted leaves
failures.symptom: Leaves droop and feel soft instead of crisp.
failures.why: Bok choy leaves lose water quickly once they are out of the cold or left uncovered. Commercial storage keeps them at 95 percent humidity or higher, far above open fridge air.
prevent: Keep it in a bag in the crisper drawer
Get it into the fridge soon after you buy it
failures.verdictNote: Still good if there is no slime or bad smell. Stand the stalks in cold water for 15 minutes to firm them back up, or just cook it.
rescue: Sauté it with garlic
Add it to soup

failures.title: Slimy, soft base
failures.symptom: The base of the stalks turns soft, wet and dark, and smells bad.
failures.why: UC Davis describes bacterial soft rot in bok choy as starting at the base of the leaves, with soft, water-soaked tissue and a foul smell. Cuts and bruises let it in.
prevent: Store it dry. Do not wash it until you cook it
Do not crush it under heavier produce
failures.verdictNote: Toss bok choy that is slimy or smells bad. If only one outer stalk is affected, pull it off and use the firm, clean stalks after a good rinse.

items.name: Collard Greens
items.intro: Collards are tough leaves, but they still yellow around ethylene and wilt when they dry out. They keep about a week.

failures.title: Leaves turning yellow
failures.symptom: Leaves lose their dark green color and turn yellow.
failures.why: USDA's storage handbook says all leafy cooking greens are sensitive to ethylene. Yellowing is the sign, and warm storage speeds it up.
prevent: Keep collards away from apples, pears and bananas
Keep them cold, in a bag
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat. Yellow leaves are more bitter, so trim the worst and cook the rest.
rescue: Simmer them low and slow
Blanch and freeze them

failures.title: Limp, wilted leaves
failures.symptom: Leaves droop and feel soft instead of crisp.
failures.why: Collard greens lose water quickly once they are out of the cold or left uncovered. Commercial storage keeps them at 95 percent humidity or higher, far above open fridge air.
prevent: Keep them in a bag in the crisper drawer
Get them into the fridge soon after you buy them
failures.verdictNote: Still good if there is no slime or bad smell. Soak the leaves in cold water for 15 minutes to firm them back up, or just cook them.
rescue: Sauté them with garlic
Add them to soup

failures.title: Slimy, dark leaves
failures.symptom: Leaves turn dark, wet and slimy, and smell bad.
failures.why: USDA's storage handbook names bacterial soft rot as the most common decay in leafy greens. It starts where leaves are bruised, wet or packed tight.
prevent: Store them dry. Do not wash them until you use them
Pick out damaged leaves before they spoil the rest
failures.verdictNote: Toss slimy or bad-smelling leaves. If only a few are affected, the crisp, clean ones are fine after a good rinse.

items.name: Swiss Chard
items.intro: Chard is more tender than kale or collards and keeps only a few days. It yellows around ethylene and wilts quickly.

failures.title: Yellow or brown leaf edges
failures.symptom: The edges of the leaves turn yellow, then brown.
failures.why: USDA's storage handbook lists yellowing and browning of the leaf edges from ethylene exposure as a main storage problem for Swiss chard.
prevent: Keep chard away from apples, pears and bananas
Keep it cold, in a bag
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat. Trim off the yellow or brown edges and cook the rest soon.
rescue: Sauté the leaves and stems with garlic
Add it to soup or beans

failures.title: Limp, wilted leaves
failures.symptom: Leaves droop and feel soft instead of crisp.
failures.why: Chard leaves lose water quickly once they are out of the cold or left uncovered. Commercial storage keeps them at 95 percent humidity or higher, far above open fridge air.
prevent: Keep it in a bag in the crisper drawer
Get it into the fridge soon after you buy it
failures.verdictNote: Still good if there is no slime or bad smell. Soak the leaves in cold water for 15 minutes to firm them back up, or just cook them.
rescue: Sauté it with garlic
Add it to soup

failures.title: Slimy, dark leaves
failures.symptom: Leaves turn dark, wet and slimy, and smell bad.
failures.why: USDA's storage handbook names bacterial soft rot as the most common decay in leafy greens. It starts where leaves are bruised, wet or packed tight.
prevent: Store it dry. Do not wash it until you use it
Pick out damaged leaves before they spoil the rest
failures.verdictNote: Toss slimy or bad-smelling leaves. If only a few are affected, the crisp, clean ones are fine after a good rinse.

items.name: Arugula
items.intro: Arugula is one of the shortest-lived greens, a few days at home. It yellows, and damp leaves turn slimy.

failures.title: Leaves turning yellow
failures.symptom: Leaves fade from green to yellow.
failures.why: USDA's storage handbook says salad greens like arugula give off very little ethylene but are highly sensitive to it, and the result is yellow leaves. Even stored well, arugula lasts 7 to 10 days from harvest.
prevent: Keep arugula away from apples, pears and bananas
Keep it cold and use it within a few days
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat. Pick out the yellow leaves and use the rest soon.
rescue: Wilt it into pasta or onto pizza
Blend it into pesto

failures.title: Slimy, dark leaves
failures.symptom: Leaves turn dark, wet and slimy, usually at the bottom of the container.
failures.why: Small, tender leaves break down fast when moisture collects in a closed container. USDA's storage handbook names bacterial soft rot as the most common decay in leafy greens.
prevent: Keep a dry paper towel in the container and change it when it gets damp
Do not wash arugula until you use it
failures.verdictNote: Toss slimy or bad-smelling leaves. If only a few are affected, the dry, clean ones are fine after a good rinse.

failures.title: Limp, wilted leaves
failures.symptom: Leaves droop and feel soft instead of crisp.
failures.why: Arugula leaves lose water quickly once they are out of the cold or left uncovered. Commercial storage keeps them at 95 percent humidity or higher, far above open fridge air.
prevent: Keep it in a bag in the crisper drawer
Get it into the fridge soon after you buy it
failures.verdictNote: Still good if there is no slime or bad smell. Soak the leaves in cold water for 10 minutes to firm them back up.
rescue: Sauté it with garlic
Add it to soup

items.name: Mustard Greens
items.intro: Mustard greens are thin and tender, so they keep only a few days. They yellow around ethylene and wilt fast.

failures.title: Leaves turning yellow
failures.symptom: Leaves lose their bright green color and turn yellow.
failures.why: USDA's storage handbook says all leafy cooking greens are sensitive to ethylene. Yellowing is the sign, and warm storage speeds it up.
prevent: Keep mustard greens away from apples, pears and bananas
Keep them cold, in a bag
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat. Trim the worst leaves and cook the rest soon.
rescue: Braise them with onion and a splash of vinegar
Blanch and freeze them

failures.title: Limp, wilted leaves
failures.symptom: Leaves droop and feel soft instead of crisp.
failures.why: Mustard greens lose water quickly once they are out of the cold or left uncovered. Commercial storage keeps them at 95 percent humidity or higher, far above open fridge air.
prevent: Keep them in a bag in the crisper drawer
Get them into the fridge soon after you buy them
failures.verdictNote: Still good if there is no slime or bad smell. Soak the leaves in cold water for 15 minutes to firm them back up, or just cook them.
rescue: Sauté them with garlic
Add them to soup

failures.title: Slimy, dark leaves
failures.symptom: Leaves turn dark, wet and slimy, and smell bad.
failures.why: USDA's storage handbook names bacterial soft rot as the most common decay in leafy greens. It starts where leaves are bruised, wet or packed tight.
prevent: Store them dry. Do not wash them until you use them
Pick out damaged leaves before they spoil the rest
failures.verdictNote: Toss slimy or bad-smelling leaves. If only a few are affected, the crisp, clean ones are fine after a good rinse.

items.name: Beet
items.intro: Beet roots keep for weeks once the greens are off. They go soft as they dry out, and the greens fade within days.

failures.title: Soft, rubbery beets
failures.symptom: The roots feel soft or wrinkled instead of hard.
failures.why: Beets go soft as they lose water, and greens left on keep pulling moisture out of the root. Commercial storage holds them at 98 percent humidity or higher.
prevent: Cut the greens off an inch above the root
Keep the roots in a bag in the crisper drawer
failures.verdictNote: Still good if there are no moldy or slimy spots and they smell fresh.
rescue: Roast them
Grate them into slaw or borscht

failures.title: Yellow, wilted greens
failures.symptom: The leafy tops turn limp and yellow while the roots are still firm.
failures.why: The tops age much faster than the roots. Storage tables give bunched beets with tops 10 to 14 days, against months for topped roots.
prevent: Cut the greens off when you get home and store them separately
Use the greens within 2 to 3 days
failures.verdictNote: Cut off and discard yellow or slimy tops. The roots are fine if they are firm.
rescue: Sauté fresh greens like chard

failures.title: Moldy or dark, soft spots
failures.symptom: Gray fuzz, or dark, wet, sunken patches, often at the tip of the root.
failures.why: USDA's storage handbook names gray mold as the most common decay in stored beets, and black rot as a second one that mostly affects the root tip.
prevent: Keep the roots dry in their bag
Check stored beets every week or so
failures.verdictNote: Beets are firm, so USDA says a small mold spot can be cut off with at least an inch around and below it. Toss a beet that is soft or slimy all the way through.

items.name: Ginger
items.intro: Ginger keeps for weeks in the fridge. It ends by shriveling as it dries out, or by molding where it was cut or stayed damp.

failures.title: Wrinkled, shriveled skin
failures.symptom: The skin wrinkles and the piece feels light and a little soft.
failures.why: USDA's storage handbook calls drying out the most common problem with stored ginger. Shriveling shows once it has lost about a tenth of its weight.
prevent: Keep it unpeeled in a bag with the air pressed out
Freeze what you will not use within a month
failures.verdictNote: Still good if the flesh inside is firm, pale yellow and smells like ginger. It will be more fibrous.
rescue: Grate it into stir-fries or tea
Slice and freeze it

failures.title: Mold on the skin or cut end
failures.symptom: Blue-green or white fuzz, usually on a cut end.
failures.why: Surface mold grows on ginger when moisture condenses on it, and cut ends are the easiest place for it to start.
prevent: Blot cut ends dry before storing
Keep a paper towel in the bag if you see condensation
failures.verdictNote: Ginger is firm, so USDA's rule for firm vegetables applies: cut off a small mold spot with at least an inch around and below it. Toss a small piece, or one where the mold is widespread.

failures.title: Soft, wet or dark inside
failures.symptom: The piece feels soft or watery, or the flesh is brown or gray when you cut it.
failures.why: USDA's storage handbook describes two storage rots in ginger: one turns the flesh brown and dry, the other turns it soft and watery.
prevent: Buy firm pieces with taut skin
Keep it dry and cold
failures.verdictNote: Toss ginger that is soft, watery or discolored inside.

items.name: Leek
items.intro: Leeks keep a week or two. They soften around ethylene, the tops wilt as they dry out, and damaged layers turn slimy.

failures.title: Soft outer layers
failures.symptom: The stalk loses its snap and the outer layers go soft.
failures.why: USDA's storage handbook rates leeks as moderately sensitive to ethylene and lists softening and more decay as the effects.
prevent: Keep leeks away from apples and pears
Keep them cold, in a bag
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat. Peel off the soft outer layer and use the firm stalk underneath soon.
rescue: Cook them into soup
Braise or roast them

failures.title: Wilted, floppy tops
failures.symptom: The green tops droop and dry out at the tips.
failures.why: USDA's storage handbook says high humidity is essential to keep leeks from wilting. Open fridge air is much drier than they need.
prevent: Keep them in a bag in the crisper drawer
Leave the tops on until you cook them
failures.verdictNote: Still good. Trim the dry tips. The white and pale green part is what most recipes use anyway.
rescue: Save the dark tops for stock

failures.title: Slimy layers
failures.symptom: Outer layers turn dark, wet and slimy, and smell bad.
failures.why: Leeks get the same soft rots as onions. They start where the stalk was bruised or stayed wet.
prevent: Store leeks unwashed
Do not crush them under heavier produce
failures.verdictNote: Toss a leek that is slimy or smells bad. If only the outermost layer is affected, peel it away and rinse the firm stalk well.

items.name: Artichoke
items.intro: Artichokes are flower buds, and they fade within a week. The leaves bruise, dry out and open up.

failures.title: Brown or black marks on the leaves
failures.symptom: Leaf tips and scuffed areas turn brown or black.
failures.why: UC Davis calls bruising and compression injury very common in artichokes. The damaged spots darken.
prevent: Handle them gently and do not pack them under heavy produce
Store them in a bag so they do not rub against other items
failures.verdictNote: Cosmetic. The heart and the base of the leaves are fine if the artichoke is still heavy and firm.
rescue: Steam or braise them
Trim the tips with scissors before cooking

failures.title: Dry, spreading leaves
failures.symptom: The artichoke feels light, and the leaves spread open and turn tough.
failures.why: Artichokes lose water and quality quickly. UC Davis notes that their look and eating quality decline rapidly, with under three weeks of storage even in ideal commercial conditions.
prevent: Keep them in a plastic bag in the crisper drawer
Cook them within a week
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there is no mold or slime. The outer leaves will be tough, so trim more of them.
rescue: Use the hearts in pasta or dip

failures.title: Gray mold or slimy spots
failures.symptom: Gray fuzz between the leaves, or soft, wet, dark patches.
failures.why: Gray mold and bacterial soft rot are the main decay problems UC Davis lists for artichokes. Both take hold when they are stored too warm.
prevent: Keep them cold
Store them unwashed
failures.verdictNote: Toss an artichoke with mold or slime. The layered leaves make it impossible to see how far it goes.

items.name: Pumpkin
items.intro: A whole cooking pumpkin keeps a month or two in a cool, dry spot. Rot gets in through a damaged rind, and cold storage pits it.

failures.title: Soft or moldy spots on the rind
failures.symptom: A soft, sunken or discolored patch on the rind, sometimes with fuzz.
failures.why: USDA's storage handbook says decay is the main cause of loss in stored pumpkins, and many different fungi cause it. A nicked rind or a missing stem is where it gets in.
prevent: Pick one with the stem attached and no cuts or soft spots
Keep pumpkins from touching each other
Check stored pumpkins every week or two
failures.verdictNote: A whole pumpkin is hard and dense, so USDA's rule for firm vegetables applies: cut off a small mold spot with at least an inch around and below it. If the rot is soft and wet, has reached the seed cavity, or smells bad, toss the pumpkin.
rescue: Cook the trimmed pumpkin the same day

failures.title: Sunken pits in the rind
failures.symptom: Sunken pits on the rind, often followed by rot once the pumpkin warms up.
failures.why: Pumpkins get chilling injury below about 50°F. USDA's storage handbook says fridge temperatures cause sunken pits and loss of flavor, and rot follows when the pumpkin comes out of the cold.
prevent: Keep whole pumpkins in a cool room, not the fridge
Bring them in from the porch before a hard frost
failures.verdictNote: Cut it open. If the flesh under the pits is firm and smells fresh, trim the pitted areas and cook it soon. Toss it if the flesh is soft, wet or moldy.
rescue: Roast it
Cook, mash and freeze it

failures.title: Cut pumpkin turning slimy
failures.symptom: The cut surface of a stored piece turns slimy, moldy or sour-smelling.
failures.why: Once the rind is cut, the wet flesh is exposed and spoils like any cut vegetable.
prevent: Wrap cut pumpkin and refrigerate it
Use it within about 5 days, or cook and freeze it
failures.verdictNote: Toss cut pumpkin that is slimy, moldy or smells off.

items.name: Okra
items.intro: Okra is one of the most perishable vegetables, two or three days at home. It bruises, dries out, and is damaged by a cold fridge.

failures.title: Brown or black ridges
failures.symptom: The ridges and tips of the pods turn brown or black.
failures.why: UC Davis says tender okra pods are easily damaged, especially on the ridges, and the damage turns into brown and black discoloration.
prevent: Handle the pods gently
Do not pack it tightly or under other produce
failures.verdictNote: Cosmetic. The pods are fine if they are still firm and not slimy.
rescue: Roast or fry it
Add it to gumbo or stew

failures.title: Dark, pitted or water-soaked spots
failures.symptom: Pods get dark sunken pits or wet-looking patches, then rot.
failures.why: Okra keeps best at 45 to 50°F, warmer than most fridges. UC Davis lists discoloration, pitting, water-soaked spots and more decay as chilling injury.
prevent: Store okra in the warmest part of the fridge, like the door
Use it within 2 to 3 days
failures.verdictNote: Cut away pitted spots and cook the pods the same day. Toss any that are soft, slimy or moldy.
rescue: Slice and sauté it

failures.title: Limp, tough pods
failures.symptom: Pods lose their snap and turn dull, limp or woody.
failures.why: UC Davis notes that young okra pods lose water very fast, and that it takes very high humidity to slow drying, toughening and loss of freshness.
prevent: Keep the pods in a loosely closed bag
Buy okra the day you plan to cook it, or the day before
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there is no slime or mold. Tough pods need longer, wetter cooking.
rescue: Stew it with tomatoes

failures.title: Slimy or moldy pods
failures.symptom: The outside of the pods turns slimy or grows fuzz.
failures.why: Wet pods rot quickly. UC Davis says decay that follows chilling or injury is probably the most common cause of loss.
prevent: Keep the pods dry and do not wash them until you cook them
failures.verdictNote: Toss okra that is slimy on the outside or moldy.

items.name: Plantain
items.intro: Plantains are used at every stage from green to black, so most of what looks like spoiling is ripening. Cold is what really damages them.

failures.title: Peel turning yellow, then black
failures.symptom: A green plantain turns yellow, then spotted, then almost fully black.
failures.why: This is ripening. Starch turns to sugar as the peel darkens, and ethylene from other fruit speeds it up.
prevent: Keep green plantains away from apples and bananas if you want them to stay green
Cook them at the stage your recipe calls for
failures.verdictNote: A black plantain is ripe, not rotten, as long as it is not moldy, leaking or sour-smelling. It is the sweetest stage for frying.
rescue: Fry ripe ones as maduros
Bake very ripe ones or mash them into batter

failures.title: Dull, gray-brown peel that will not ripen
failures.symptom: The peel turns dull, smoky or brown and the fruit stays hard.
failures.why: UC Davis lists a dull or smoky peel, browning and failure to ripen as chilling injury in plantains kept at 45°F or colder for about a week.
prevent: Keep green plantains on the counter, never in the fridge
Only refrigerate plantains that are already fully ripe
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there is no mold. It will not sweeten, so cook it as a green plantain.
rescue: Boil it or fry it as tostones

failures.title: Brown, bruised flesh
failures.symptom: Brown patches in the flesh, sometimes with no mark on the peel.
failures.why: UC Davis notes that dropping a plantain can brown the flesh with or without damage to the skin, and that the damaged spots can then mold.
prevent: Handle them gently
Do not stack heavy items on them
failures.verdictNote: Cut away the bruised part and use the rest. Toss it if the bruise is moldy or smells fermented.
rescue: Fry or boil the rest

failures.title: Mold at the stem or tip
failures.symptom: Fuzzy mold at the stem end, or a dry, dark, rotted tip.
failures.why: UC Davis lists crown rot, stem-end rot and cigar-end rot as the main plantain diseases. They start at the cut stem or the tip and grow into the fruit.
prevent: Keep them dry, with air around them
Use ripe plantains within a few days
failures.verdictNote: Toss a plantain if mold or rot has reached the flesh. A little surface mold on the dry stem of an otherwise firm plantain peels away with the skin.

items.name: Tomatillo
items.intro: Tomatillos keep a week or two in their husks. They turn yellow and sweet as they ripen, and damp husks mold.

failures.title: Turning yellow and soft
failures.symptom: Bright green fruit turns pale, then yellow, and softens.
failures.why: Tomatillos are picked green. UC Davis notes that overripe ones turn light green or yellow and get sweeter, which most recipes do not want, and that ethylene causes the same color change.
prevent: Keep them cold, in their husks
Keep them away from apples and bananas
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if it is not moldy or mushy. It will be sweeter and less tart.
rescue: Roast them for a milder salsa
Simmer them into chile verde

failures.title: Moldy or slimy husks
failures.symptom: The papery husk turns damp, dark or fuzzy.
failures.why: UC Davis notes that surface molds grow on tomatillo husks in humid storage, and that moisture trapped inside the husk is hard to get rid of.
prevent: Store them in a paper bag, not a sealed plastic one
Keep the husks dry
failures.verdictNote: Peel off the husk. If the fruit underneath is firm and clean, wash it well and use it. Toss it if the fruit itself is moldy or soft.
rescue: Use them the same day

failures.title: Sunken pits or black mold on the fruit
failures.symptom: Small sunken pits on the skin, sometimes with black mold.
failures.why: UC Davis reports chilling injury in tomatillos after about three weeks at 41°F, sooner when colder: pitting, decay and black mold.
prevent: Use refrigerated tomatillos within a week or two
Keep them out of the coldest part of the fridge
failures.verdictNote: Toss tomatillos with mold or soft, sunken rot.

items.name: Persimmon
items.intro: There are two kinds, and they fail differently. Squat Fuyu are eaten firm and go soft around ethylene. Acorn-shaped Hachiya are not ready until they are jelly-soft.

failures.title: Firm persimmons going soft
failures.symptom: A crisp Fuyu turns soft within days.
failures.why: UC Davis rates persimmons as very sensitive to ethylene. At room temperature, 1 part per million softens them past the point stores can sell them in 6 days, and 10 parts per million does it in 2.
prevent: Keep Fuyu persimmons away from apples, pears and bananas
Keep them in the coldest part of the fridge
failures.verdictNote: A soft persimmon is safe and sweet. Toss it if it smells fermented or is moldy.
rescue: Eat it with a spoon
Use the pulp in bread, muffins or smoothies

failures.title: Chalky, mouth-puckering taste
failures.symptom: The fruit looks ripe but dries out your mouth when you bite it.
failures.why: Hachiya-type persimmons are astringent until they are completely soft. This is an unripe fruit, not a spoiled one.
prevent: Ripen Hachiya on the counter until they feel like a water balloon
Put them in a paper bag with an apple to speed it up
failures.verdictNote: Not harmful, just unpleasant. Give it more time on the counter.
rescue: Once soft, scoop out the pulp and freeze it for baking

failures.title: Brown, mushy flesh after cold storage
failures.symptom: A Fuyu looks fine outside but the flesh is brown and soft.
failures.why: UC Davis says Fuyu-type persimmons get chilling injury between 41 and 59°F, with flesh browning and softening, and that ethylene makes it worse. Colder than that, near freezing, is safe.
prevent: Keep Fuyu in the coldest part of the fridge, not the door
Eat them within a few weeks
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if it smells fine and has no mold. The texture suffers, so bake with it.
rescue: Use it in bread or pudding

failures.title: Mold on the skin or under the cap
failures.symptom: Black or fuzzy spots on the skin or around the green cap.
failures.why: Mold gets in through cracks and at the cap, and it spreads quickly in soft, ripe fruit.
prevent: Keep them dry
Use ripe persimmons within a day or two
failures.verdictNote: Toss a moldy persimmon. It is a soft fruit, so mold reaches past what you can see.

items.name: Parsnip
items.intro: Parsnips keep for weeks. When they fail it is usually a bitter taste from ethylene, or going limp as they dry out.

failures.title: Bitter taste
failures.symptom: The parsnips look fine but taste bitter.
failures.why: USDA's storage handbook says even low levels of ethylene in cold storage make parsnips bitter. An apple or pear in the same drawer is a source.
prevent: Keep parsnips away from apples, pears and other fruit
Store them in a bag in the crisper drawer
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat. Cooking them with something sweet balances the bitterness.
rescue: Roast them with honey or maple
Blend them into soup with apple or carrot

failures.title: Limp, rubbery parsnips
failures.symptom: The roots bend instead of snapping and may look shriveled.
failures.why: Parsnips go rubbery when they lose water. Commercial storage keeps them at 98 percent humidity.
prevent: Cut off any green tops
Keep them in a closed bag in the crisper drawer
failures.verdictNote: Still good. Soak them in cold water for an hour to firm them back up.
rescue: Roast them
Simmer them in soup or stew

failures.title: Brown patches on the skin
failures.symptom: Tan or brown areas on the surface of the root.
failures.why: USDA's storage handbook ties surface browning in parsnips mostly to bruising and scuffing, and notes it increases the longer they are stored.
prevent: Handle them gently
Use older parsnips first
failures.verdictNote: Cosmetic. Peel them and they are fine, as long as the flesh is firm.
rescue: Peel and roast them

failures.title: Moldy or slimy spots
failures.symptom: Gray fuzz, or soft, wet, sunken patches.
failures.why: Gray mold, bacterial soft rot and watery soft rot all attack stored parsnips. Damaged roots get them first.
prevent: Keep the bag free of standing water
Check stored parsnips every week or so
failures.verdictNote: Parsnips are firm, so USDA says a small mold spot can be cut off with at least an inch around and below it. Toss one that is slimy or soft all the way through.

items.name: Turnip
items.intro: Turnips keep for weeks in the cold. They shrivel as they dry out, and warm storage brings on soft rot.

failures.title: Soft, shriveled turnips
failures.symptom: The roots feel spongy or look wrinkled.
failures.why: Turnips shrivel as they lose water. USDA's storage handbook says to keep them cold and at high humidity to slow it, and that storage above 41°F speeds up weight loss.
prevent: Cut off the greens
Keep the roots in a bag in the crisper drawer
failures.verdictNote: Still good if there are no dark, soft spots and they smell fresh.
rescue: Roast them
Mash them with potatoes

failures.title: Soft, wet or moldy spots
failures.symptom: Soft, watery, sunken patches, sometimes with gray fuzz.
failures.why: USDA's storage handbook says storing turnips warmer than 41°F speeds up soft rot. Gray mold and watery soft rot are also listed.
prevent: Keep them cold
Keep them dry in their bag
failures.verdictNote: Turnips are firm, so USDA says a small mold spot can be cut off with at least an inch around and below it. Toss one that is slimy or soft all the way through.

failures.title: Yellow, wilted greens
failures.symptom: The leafy tops turn limp and yellow while the roots are still firm.
failures.why: The tops age much faster than the roots. USDA's storage handbook calls turnip greens particularly perishable.
prevent: Cut the greens off when you get home and store them separately
Use the greens within 2 to 3 days
failures.verdictNote: Cut off and discard yellow or slimy tops. The roots are fine if they are firm.
rescue: Cook fresh greens like mustard greens

items.name: Fennel
items.intro: Fennel keeps about a week. Cut and bruised surfaces brown, and the bulb goes limp as it dries out.

failures.title: Brown cuts and bruises
failures.symptom: The cut base and any scuffed spots on the bulb turn brown.
failures.why: USDA's storage handbook says mechanical injury produces rapid browning in fennel, and that stores trim brown cut surfaces and injured outer layers.
prevent: Handle the bulb gently
Slice it just before you use it
failures.verdictNote: Cosmetic. Shave off the brown surface or peel away the outer layer. The rest is fine if it is firm.
rescue: Shave it into salad
Roast or braise it

failures.title: Limp, rubbery bulb
failures.symptom: The bulb loses its crunch and the layers feel soft.
failures.why: Fennel is crisp because it is full of water. USDA's storage handbook recommends 90 to 95 percent humidity and gives it about two weeks even in ideal commercial storage.
prevent: Keep the bulb in a bag in the crisper drawer
Cut off the stalks, which pull moisture from the bulb
failures.verdictNote: Safe to eat if there is no slime or bad smell. It has lost its crunch, so cook it.
rescue: Braise it
Add it to soup or roast it with other vegetables

failures.title: Slimy or moldy spots
failures.symptom: Soft, wet, dark patches, or fuzz between the layers.
failures.why: Like other fresh vegetables, fennel rots where it was bruised or stayed wet.
prevent: Store it dry and unwashed
Use it within a week
failures.verdictNote: Toss fennel that is slimy or smells bad. If only the outer layer is affected, peel it away and rinse the firm bulb underneath well.
